MILLET FLOUR & READY-MIX PRODUCTION SYSTEM

The Super Production Workflow — one merged, decision-gated sequence for 7 flours and 3 ready mixes

Phase 1: 25-50 kg/day micro unit  •  designed to scale to 150 kg/day  •  India, September 2026

Before anything else — three time-critical alerts

1. PMFME subsidy closes 30 September 2026 — four days from today. The credit-linked capital subsidy (35% of eligible project cost, ceiling Rs 10 lakh per micro unit) runs 2020-21 to 2025-26 with a stated end date of 30 Sep 2026; it has already hit its 2 lakh-unit target and an extension with revised norms has been publicly flagged as likely but is not something you can rely on. Call your District PMFME Resource Person and your bank today, and simultaneously prepare your DPR so you can file the day any extension is notified. Also ask your state about a millet value-addition scheme and any Common Facility Centre within 100 km — renting destoning, roasting, grinding and packing time per kg can cut your Phase-1 capex by 40-60%.
2. FSSAI turnover thresholds changed with effect from 01.04.2026. Per the FoSCoS "Kind of Business Eligibility" document updated 01.04.2026: Registration now covers annual turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore (previously Rs 12 lakh); State Licence covers Rs 1.5-50 crore; Central Licence above Rs 50 crore and for importers/exporters. Confirm your exact kind-of-business code on FoSCoS before applying — applying for the wrong category wastes months.
3. Do not launch all ten SKUs on day one. Launch four or five (Ragi, Jowar, Sprouted Ragi, Malt Mix, Dosa Mix). Ten SKUs means ten label artworks, ten lab nutrition panels, ten pouch designs and ten recipes to master. Four means you can actually be excellent, keep finished stock under 30 days, and let freshness — your only defensible advantage over unbranded mandi flour — do the selling.

The 10 products

Four process families, one spine. The differences are parameters, not machines.

Family A - Plain Millet Flours

Ragi Flour (Finger Millet)

Route
S01-S02-S03-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
MANDATORY. Drum roaster, grain temp 100-110 C, 15-20 min, batch 10-15 kg.
End point: grains 1 shade lighter, crackle stops, strong chocolate/nutty aroma, moisture 4-6%.
Why: inactivates lipase + amylase -> shelf life jumps from ~2 months to 6-9 months; kills raw 'green' taste.
Grind
Pulveriser, 60-mesh (250 micron) screen -> target 98% passing 60 mesh.
Alternative positioning: stone chakki (2-3 HP) for a 'stone-ground, low-heat' premium SKU. Coarser (~40-60 mesh), better roti texture.
Moisture max
<=9.0% (internal target 8.0%). Water activity aw <=0.55.
Shelf life
9 months (plain), 12 months if foil + O2 absorber + store <25 C
Pack + O₂ absorber
250 g / 500 g pouch, 1 kg bag — Optional 50 cc sachet (extends shelf life ~2 months, costs Re 0.70-1.50/pack). Mandatory only for bajra.
Key risk
Under-roasting -> rancidity in month 4-5. Grinding hot -> condensation inside pouch -> mould. Buying high-moisture ragi in monsoon -> clumping + mould.
Family A - Plain Millet Flours

Jowar Flour (Sorghum)

Route
S01-S02-S03-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
LIGHT ROAST ONLY (decide by channel):
- Retail pouch, 6-9 month shelf life -> roast 100-105 C, 10-12 min (recommended, this is your default).
- Fresh-sale / roti-shop supply -> may skip roast, but shelf life drops to 4-6 weeks.
End point: cream colour unchanged to very light tan, popcorn-like aroma, moisture 5-7%. Do NOT brown jowar.
Grind
Pulveriser, 60-mesh screen -> 98% passing 60 mesh. Jowar is soft; do not overfeed or you get fine dust that packs hard.
Moisture max
<=9.0% (target 8.0%), aw <=0.55
Shelf life
9 months (roasted, foil pouch)
Pack + O₂ absorber
250 g / 500 g / 1 kg — Optional 50 cc.
Key risk
Mouldy grey/black jowar lots = aflatoxin. Reject at intake, do not 'clean and use'. Over-roasting turns jowar grey-brown and bitter - customers notice immediately.
Family B - Sprouted Flours

Sprouted Ragi Flour

Route
S01-S02-S03-S04-S05-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
GENTLE. Drum roaster 90-100 C, 8-12 min only. This is a 'stabilisation roast', not a flavour roast.
End point: aroma turns malty/sweet like malted milk drink, colour unchanged, moisture <=5%.
Above 105 C you lose the sprouted nutrition claim - and that claim is the entire reason this SKU costs more.
Grind
Pulveriser, 80-mesh (180 micron) screen -> finer than plain ragi, because it is sold as a malt/health product.
Sprouted grain is more friable, so throughput is ~20% higher and motor load lower. Reduce feed rate by 20% anyway to keep flour <40 C.
Moisture max
<=8.0% (tighter than plain flour), aw <=0.50
Shelf life
6 months (sprouted products always carry a shorter shelf life than plain - be honest on the label)
Pack + O₂ absorber
200 g / 400 g / 500 g (premium pricing, smaller packs sell better) — Recommended 50 cc - sprouted flour has higher free sugar and enzyme activity, so it oxidises faster.
Key risk
MICROBIAL - this is your single highest food-safety risk. Warm + wet + 36 h = Salmonella / Bacillus cereus / E. coli paradise.
Controls: potable (preferably RO/UV) water only, 200 ppm chlorine sanitised trays, no water pooling, room temp never >30 C, dry within 30 min of sprout completion, and TEST EVERY BATCH (TPC / yeast-mould / coliform / E. coli / Salmonella).
Second risk: over-sprouting -> bitter, low yield.
Third risk: skipping the micro test -> one recall kills a new brand.
Family B - Sprouted Flours

Sprouted Jowar Flour

Route
S01-S02-S03-S04-S05-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
Gentle stabilisation roast 90-100 C, 8-10 min. End: malty aroma, colour unchanged, moisture <=5%.
Grind
Pulveriser, 80-mesh screen. Jowar sprouts grind slightly fluffier than ragi - keep feed rate low to avoid 'choking' the cyclone.
Moisture max
<=8.0%, aw <=0.50
Shelf life
6 months
Pack + O₂ absorber
200 g / 400 g / 500 g — Recommended 50 cc.
Key risk
Same microbial risk as sprouted ragi. Plus: jowar sprouts mat together faster than ragi, so turn the tray every rinse or you get a solid cake with a wet, sour centre.
Family C - High-Fat / Dehusked Flours

Bajra Flour (Pearl Millet)

Route
S01-S02-S03-(S06)-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
MANDATORY AND THE MOST CRITICAL STEP IN THE WHOLE PLANT FOR THIS SKU.
Drum roaster, grain temp 110-120 C, 15-20 min, batch max 10 kg (bajra scorches easily).
End point: light golden-brown, strong roasted-nut aroma, moisture <=4%, and a 'bite test' that is crisp not chewy.
Why: bajra has 5-6% fat and very active lipase. Unroasted bajra flour goes bitter/rancid in 10-15 DAYS at room temperature. Proper dry-heat treatment extends it to 3-4 months.
Grind
Pulveriser, 60-mesh screen. GRIND IN SMALL LOTS AND IMMEDIATELY PACK.
Bajra flour must not sit in an open bin. Grind -> sift -> fill -> seal within the same 2 hours.
Moisture max
<=7.0% - the tightest spec in your range. Target 6%.
Shelf life
4 months maximum. Print 4 months. Do not be greedy - a rancid pack destroys the brand for the other 9 SKUs too.
Pack + O₂ absorber
200 g / 500 g (do not sell 1 kg bajra flour until you have proven shelf life) — MANDATORY 100 cc sachet in every 500 g pack. This is the single cheapest shelf-life insurance you can buy (Re 1-2 per pack).
Key risk
RANCIDITY. Bajra is the SKU most likely to fail in the market.
Controls: (1) roast properly at 110-120 C, (2) cool fast, (3) grind-to-order, (4) foil pouch + 100 cc O2 absorber, (5) store finished packs below 25 C, (6) run a peroxide value / free fatty acid test at day 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 on every new roast profile.
Family C - High-Fat / Dehusked Flours

Rajgira Flour (Amaranth)

Route
S01-S02-S03-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
VERY LIGHT. Drum roaster 85-95 C, 4-6 min, batch max 5 kg.
Rajgira seeds are 1 mm across - they scorch in seconds. Keep the drum turning fast and never walk away.
End point: faint nutty smell, colour barely changed, one or two seeds may pop. Moisture <=4%.
Alternative: skip roasting and grind raw, then shelf life drops to 3-4 months. Roasting is recommended.
Grind
THIS IS THE HARDEST SKU TO GRIND. Rajgira is ~7% oil; continuous grinding turns it into a paste (like peanut butter) that coats the beaters.
Method: (1) use the coarsest screen you can accept (40-60 mesh), (2) feed at HALF the normal rate, (3) grind in 2-minute bursts with 1-minute pauses, (4) purge the mill with 1 kg of dry jowar afterwards and keep that purge flour separate as 'cleaning flour' (do not sell it as rajgira), (5) if it still pastes, blend 20% roasted jowar flour in DURING grinding as a carrier, then adjust the label to a 'Rajgira-Millet Flour'.
Moisture max
<=7.0%, aw <=0.45
Shelf life
6 months (roasted + foil + O2 absorber). 4 months if unroasted.
Pack + O₂ absorber
100 g / 200 g (premium, small packs - the market will not buy 500 g of a Rs 180/kg flour yet) — MANDATORY 50 cc.
Key risk
(1) Oiling up / pasting inside the mill - the top operational headache. (2) Rancidity - smells like old paint or putty. (3) Sand. A gritty rajgira pack gets returned instantly. (4) High raw-material cost means high waste cost - track yield daily.
Family C - High-Fat / Dehusked Flours

Kuttu Flour (Buckwheat)

Route
S01-S02-S03-S07-S08-S09-S10-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
LIGHT. Drum roaster 90-100 C, 6-10 min, batch max 8 kg.
End point: aroma changes from raw-beany to warm/nutty, colour goes from pale green to light tan. Moisture <=5%.
Note: a large part of the Indian market expects kuttu to be raw for vrat (fasting) use. Consider TWO sub-SKUs: 'Kuttu Flour (Roasted)' for shelf life and 'Kuttu Flour (Raw, Navratri grade)' sold only in Sep-Oct with a 3-month shelf life.
Grind
Pulveriser, 60-mesh screen. Kuttu is softer than ragi but also slightly oily (~3.4%). Feed at 70% of normal rate. Watch for the flour turning grey-green - that means it is heating too much.
Moisture max
<=8.0%, aw <=0.50
Shelf life
6 months roasted | 3 months raw
Pack + O₂ absorber
100 g / 200 g / 500 g — Recommended 50 cc.
Key risk
(1) Stones - kuttu is sold with stones and they break teeth. Hand-pick AND destone AND magnet AND sieve. Four layers.
(2) Price volatility - never buy more than 6 weeks of stock at peak price.
(3) Black specks from husk - a visual defect customers photograph and post.
Family D - Ready Mixes

Sprouted Ragi Malt Mix

Route
S01-S02-S03 (purchased ingredients only) -> S07/S09/S10 (component roasting & grinding) -> S11-S12-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
Not applicable (ingredients arrive roasted)
Grind
Component flours are already at 80 mesh. No re-grinding. If the malt powder is coarse, pass it through the pulveriser on 80 mesh first.
Moisture max
<=6.0% - the tightest in the range, because milk powder and jaggery both grab water and cause caking.
Shelf life
6 months (9 months if no milk powder is used)
Pack + O₂ absorber
200 g / 400 g / 500 g stand-up zipper pouch, or 400 g PET jar for premium gifting — Recommended 50 cc.
Key risk
(1) Caking / lumping - jaggery powder and milk powder are hygroscopic. Blend room humidity must be <=55% RH or do not run.
(2) MILK POWDER changes everything: it makes this a dairy-containing product -> allergen declaration mandatory, vegetarian mark still OK, but shelf life drops and microbial risk rises. Consider a 'vegan / no-milk' version as your default and a 'with milk powder' premium version.
(3) Diastatic vs non-diastatic malt: diastatic malt has active enzymes that will keep working in the pack and thin the malt drink over time. Use NON-DIASTATIC (heat-treated) malt powder for a shelf-stable premix.
(4) Do not print 'baby food' or any disease claim.
Family D - Ready Mixes

Multi Millet Health Mix

Route
S01-S02-S03 (purchased ingredients only) -> S07/S09/S10 (component roasting & grinding) -> S11-S12-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
Roast the pulses, nuts and gond separately (S07) before blending. Do not roast the blended mix - you will destroy the sprouted flours.
Grind
Pulses, nuts and dalia are ground separately on an 80-mesh screen before blending.
Nuts: grind in 20-second bursts with 1 tbsp of the base flour as a carrier, or you get nut butter instead of powder.
Moisture max
<=6.0%, aw <=0.45
Shelf life
6 months with nuts | 9 months nut-free
Pack + O₂ absorber
250 g / 500 g / 1 kg pouch — MANDATORY 100 cc if it contains nuts (nuts go rancid fast).
Key risk
(1) ALLERGENS - groundnut and almond. If you make a nut-free version on the same blender, you MUST (a) run nut-free FIRST in the day, (b) do a documented full wet-clean after the nut batch, (c) print 'Processed in a facility that also handles nuts / May contain traces of nuts' on EVERY pack.
(2) NUT RANCIDITY - test peroxide value at 0/60/120 days.
(3) FORTIFICATION - if you add vitamins/minerals, the product may fall under 'Health Supplements / Nutraceuticals' (FSSAI Reg 2016) with different label rules. Do not add fortificants until you have written advice from a food-tech consultant.
Family D - Ready Mixes

Millet Dosa Mix

Route
S01-S02-S03 (purchased ingredients only) -> S07/S09/S10 (component roasting & grinding) -> S11-S12-S13-S14-S15-S16-S17-S18-S19-S20
Roast / heat
Millet flours: 100-105 C, 10-12 min (as for FL-JOWAR-02).
Poha: light roast 90 C, 3-4 min, or use as-is.
URAD DAL FLOUR: DO NOT ROAST. Roasting kills the proteins that trap air and give a crispy dosa.
Grind
Two different grinds in the same product - this is the trick:
Millet flours + roasted poha -> 40-60 mesh (COARSE, rava-like). This gives the dosa its grip and crispness.
Urad dal -> 80-100 mesh (FINE). This gives the foam.
Methi + salt -> 80 mesh.
Grind the coarse part first, then the fine part, and blend. Never grind everything to 80 mesh or you get a rubbery dosa.
Moisture max
<=8.0%, aw <=0.50
Shelf life
9 months (instant type, soda included) | 6 months (ferment type, more urad = more fat)
Pack + O₂ absorber
200 g / 500 g / 1 kg — Optional 50 cc.
Key risk
(1) Particle-size segregation in the pack - the coarse fraction settles to the bottom during transport. Fix: keep the size range narrow (no big chunks), do not over-blend, and print 'Shake the pack well before use' on the front.
(2) Soda hot-spots -> yellow/bitter patches in the dosa. Fix: geometric dilution of the soda 1:20 with jowar flour before it goes in the blender.
(3) Customer failure, not product failure: too-thin batter, cold tawa, no oil. Your back-of-pack method must be photographed and idiot-proof - batter consistency, resting time, tawa temperature, spread technique. A 4-photo strip on the back panel is worth more than any amount of marketing.

The super workflow at a glance

The super workflow, stage by stage (open each for the full execution detail)

S01  —  Raw Material Sourcing & Supplier Approval  | ALL 10 SKUs | One-time 3-4 weeks to build the list; then 30 min per lot
Purpose
Lock grain QUALITY and CONSISTENCY before it ever reaches your gate. Every downstream defect - grit, rancidity, mould, poor sprouting - is decided at this step. It is the cheapest step to do well and the most expensive to fix later.
Inputs
Approved-vendor list, written purchase specification sheet, moisture meter, 1 kg sample bags, purchase order template
Outputs
Signed vendor agreement + approved vendor list + purchase specification per grain
Critical parameters
Spec-per-grain written | >=3 suppliers per grain | baseline lab report on file | vendor agreement signed
Automation level
MANUAL (100%)
How to automate it
No machine can buy good grain. Tools only: a Rs 2,500-8,000 grain moisture meter and a Rs 3,000 lab send-out.
Machines / equipment
Manual work remaining
Owner / purchase in-charge. 2-3 days per grain, once a year, plus 30 minutes per new lot.
Quality checks
Baseline lab report per grain (one time). Germination test for sprouting grain. Moisture check on every lot.

Step by step

  1. 1. Write a one-page PURCHASE SPEC for each of the 5 grains you buy (ragi, jowar, bajra, rajgira, kuttu) plus urad dal, poha, chana dal, jaggery, nuts, spices. Spec = variety, moisture %, foreign matter %, broken %, colour, odour, packaging (50 kg new PP bags with liner), season, and 'must be free from insect damage, mould and rodent contamination'.
  2. 2. Identify 3 suppliers per grain: (a) an FPO / farmer producer company, (b) a mandi wholesaler / commission agent, (c) an IndiaMART-listed trader. Never single-source.
  3. 3. Buy a 1-2 kg SAMPLE from each and evaluate: moisture meter reading, 100-grain visual count of defective grains, float test in water, sand-grind test (chew a pinch - listen/feel for grit), smell test, and for ragi/jowar a 100-grain GERMINATION test if you plan to sprout it.
  4. 4. Send one sample of each grain to an NABL food lab for a baseline test: moisture, total ash, acid-insoluble ash (sand), heavy metals (lead, cadmium, arsenic), aflatoxin B1, and a pesticide-residue screen. Budget Rs 4,000-9,000 per grain, one time. This becomes your supplier scorecard.
  5. 5. Ask each shortlisted supplier for: FSSAI licence copy, GST certificate, bank details, and 2 customer references you can phone.
  6. 6. Do a supplier audit - at micro scale a 45-minute VIDEO CALL walking through their cleaning/grading line and store is acceptable. For a >Rs 5 lakh/year supplier, visit in person once.
  7. 7. Fix payment terms (aim 50% advance / 50% on delivery after QC), a rejection clause ('lot rejected if moisture > 13% or visible mould; freight borne by supplier'), and a price-review cycle.
  8. 8. Sign a one-page vendor agreement and add the supplier to your Approved Vendor List with a review date 12 months later.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Supplier passes spec + lab + audit
THEN APPROVE -> add to Approved Vendor List -> raise PO -> proceed to S02
IF Supplier fails on price only
THEN Keep as backup, renegotiate at the next harvest window
IF Supplier fails lab (heavy metals / aflatoxin / pesticide above FSSAI limits)
THEN REJECT PERMANENTLY for that grain. Do not 'blend it down'.
IF No supplier reaches >=90% germination for sprouting-grade ragi/jowar
THEN Either (a) buy from a specialised sprouting-grade supplier even at +Rs 5-8/kg, or (b) run the hybrid route: buy certified pre-sprouted / malted flour from an approved processor for the sprouted SKUs until you find grain that works. Document which route you chose.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Buying from an unverified mandi trader because he is Rs 3/kg cheaper
→ Rs 3/kg saved, Rs 40/kg lost in rejects, re-cleaning and one bad batch that kills your brand. Never do it.
✗ No written spec
→ Every lot arrives different; your roast profile never stabilises; operators blame the machine.
✗ Buying 2-year-old grain for sprouting
→ Germination <40%. You will spend 3 days sprouting and get nothing. Always run the 100-grain test.
✗ Single sourcing
→ One failed crop and your plant stops. Minimum 2 live suppliers per grain.
S02  —  Goods Inward, Intake QC & Warehousing  | ALL 10 SKUs | 30-45 min per truck
Purpose
Physically receive, verify, code and store the grain so that (a) you are not cheated on weight, (b) every bag is traceable to a lot code, and (c) the grain does not deteriorate while it waits.
Inputs
Truck / tempo, 50 kg bags, platform scale, moisture meter, grain trier or sampling probe, status labels, pallets
Outputs
GRN (Goods Received Note) + lot-coded, QC-status-labelled, palletised raw store
Critical parameters
Weight tolerance +-0.5% | sample >=10% of bags | moisture recorded | lot code on every bag | GREEN/AMBER/RED status | store <=30 C, <=60% RH | FIFO
Automation level
MANUAL (95%) - only weighing and moisture reading are 'instrumented'
How to automate it
Platform scale 300 kg x 20 g (Rs 8-18k) with a printer/RS232 so the weight prints on the GRN. Handheld grain moisture meter (Rs 2.5-8k).
Machines / equipment
Platform scale; moisture meter; grain trier; pallets; thermo-hygrometer
Manual work remaining
1 helper + QC person. 30-45 minutes per 50-bag truck.
Quality checks
Moisture on every lot. Floaters on every lot. Full lab panel once per supplier per quarter.

Step by step

  1. 1. Unload into the INTAKE area only. This area must be physically separate from the processing and packing areas, and ideally at a different door.
  2. 2. Weigh the full vehicle on a platform scale (or weigh every 10th bag and multiply, then re-weigh the total). Record gross, tare, net. Tolerance +-0.5% of the invoice; outside that, dispute before signing.
  3. 3. SAMPLE properly: for a lot up to 50 bags, probe at least 10% of the bags (min 5 bags) using a grain trier from top, middle and bottom of each. Mix into one 2 kg composite sample. A handful off the top of one bag is not a sample.
  4. 4. TEST the composite: moisture meter (3 readings, average them), visual foreign matter on a white tray, smell, and the float test (100 g grain in 500 ml water + 1 tsp salt - floaters are hollow/insect-damaged; count them, aim <=3%).
  5. 5. Check for live infestation: pour 500 g on a white sheet, look for weevils, moths, webbing and 'hot spots'. Also open 2 bags and look inside the folds - moth larvae hide there.
  6. 6. Assign a LOT CODE and write it on every bag with a paint marker or a printed sticker. Format: RM-<grain>-YYMMDD-<supplier code>-<seq>. Example: RM-RAGI-260926-KFPO1-01.
  7. 7. Apply a STATUS LABEL to every bag - GREEN 'ACCEPTED', AMBER 'UNDER TEST', RED 'REJECTED'. No bag moves to production without a GREEN label. This single habit prevents 90% of accidental use of bad material.
  8. 8. Enter everything into the RAW MATERIAL REGISTER (Excel): lot code, supplier, PO no, invoice no, date, bags, net weight, moisture %, floater %, foreign matter %, status, QC-by, released-by.
  9. 9. Store on pallets: 15 cm off the floor, 45 cm off the walls, 60 cm gap between stacks for inspection and pest baiting. Bags stacked max 8 high (cross-stacked, not column-stacked, so the pile does not split).
  10. 10. Store conditions: cool, dry, dark, ventilated. Target <=30 C and <=60% RH. Put a Rs 300 wall thermo-hygrometer in the room and log it twice daily. NO raw grain in the same room as finished packs, ever.
  11. 11. Rotate strictly FIFO. Write the lot code and receipt date on a whiteboard 'stock board' by the door so anyone can see what is oldest.
  12. 12. Keep the retained 1 kg sample of every lot in a sealed jar, labelled, for the life of that lot + 3 months.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Moisture <=12.5%, floaters <=3%, foreign matter <=1%, no live insects, no mould, no off-odour
THEN ACCEPT -> GREEN label -> release to raw store -> S03
IF Moisture 12.6 - 14.0%, everything else fine
THEN ACCEPT WITH CONDITIONS -> negotiate a price deduction (typical 1-2% per 0.5% moisture) -> send to S05 tray drying at 55-60 C for 1-2 h BEFORE cleaning -> re-test moisture -> then S03
IF Moisture > 14.0%
THEN REJECT or return to supplier. Do not try to dry it - above 14% mould has almost certainly already started.
IF Live insects / webbing / hot spots
THEN REJECT. Do not fumigate yourself without a licensed pest contractor, and never fumigate inside the production building.
IF Visible mould, grey/black grains, musty or chemical smell (paint, diesel, pesticide)
THEN REJECT IMMEDIATELY. Mould means aflatoxin; chemical smell means contamination that no process removes. Photograph, note the lot, inform the supplier in writing the same day.
IF Weight short by more than 0.5%
THEN Do not sign the delivery challan. Note the shortage on the challan, photograph the scale reading, and raise a debit note.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Accepting without a moisture reading
→ The most common way a new unit loses money. 1% extra moisture = 1% you paid for as grain but got as water, plus a mould risk.
✗ No lot code on bags
→ If a customer complains in month 5 you cannot trace back. That turns a 1-batch recall into a full-brand recall.
✗ Bags on the floor against the wall
→ Rats, moisture wicking, and no inspection access. Guaranteed FSSAI finding.
✗ Raw grain stored with finished packs
→ Insects walk from raw to finished. Separate rooms or at minimum a solid partition and separate air.
S03  —  Cleaning, Destoning, Grading & Aspiration  | ALL 10 SKUs (mandatory - no exceptions, not even for 'clean-looking' grain) | 100-150 kg/h
Purpose
Remove stones, sand, dust, chaff, weed seeds, insect-damaged and broken grains, and ferrous metal. One 3 mm stone that reaches the pulveriser will chip a beater, put a steel fragment in your flour, and can cost you a recall.
Inputs
Lot-coded GREEN-labelled grain, destoner-cum-grader-cum-aspirator, magnets, test sieves, SS trays, weighing scale
Outputs
'Clean grain' with foreign matter <=0.5%, lot code carried forward, cleaning loss recorded
Critical parameters
Feed rate 100-150 kg/h | foreign matter in output <=0.5% | cleaning loss 1-2% (millets), 2-6% (kuttu/rajgira) | magnet pass every batch | purge between grains
Automation level
AUTOMATED (85%) - the machine does the separation; humans set it, feed it and verify
How to automate it
Destoner-cum-Grader-cum-Aspirator, 100-250 kg/h, SS304 contact parts, 1.5-3 HP, single- or three-phase. This ONE machine replaces 3 manual operations (winnowing, sieving, stone-picking) and is the single best-value machine in the entire plant. Budget Rs 75,000 - 2,00,000.
Machines / equipment
Destoner-cum-grader-cum-aspirator (Nabhitha / Perfura / Amarun / Pilot Agrotech) | rare-earth magnetic grate or sleeved magnet | IS test sieves 1.5 / 2 / 3.5 / 4 / 5 mm | 300 kg platform scale | SS trays
Manual work remaining
1 operator. 100-150 kg per hour. Plus 10 minutes of setting and 15 minutes of cleaning per changeover.
Quality checks
500 g white-tray check every batch. Foreign matter % every batch. Magnet inspection every batch. Stone-cup check every run.

Step by step

  1. 1. Pre-inspect: dump 20-25 kg onto a large stainless or white-Formica tray. Remove by hand any string, jute fibre, large stones, lumps of mud, dead insects and clumps. Two minutes here saves a machine jam.
  2. 2. Set the machine BEFORE you start: choose the sieve sizes for the grain (ragi = fine, top screen 3.5-4 mm / bottom 1.5 mm; jowar & bajra = medium, 4-5 mm / 2 mm; kuttu = 4 mm / 2 mm; rajgira = 1.5 mm / 0.8 mm or use a dedicated fine aspirator only). Set the aspiration to the lowest setting first - you can always increase it, but too much aspiration blows good grain out with the chaff.
  3. 3. Start the machine EMPTY and run 30 seconds. Listen for rattle or rubbing. Check the stone reject cup is fitted and empty.
  4. 4. Feed at a steady, even rate - 100 to 150 kg/h for a small machine. Do not dump the whole bag at once; choking the feed makes stones ride over into the clean outlet. Use the hopper slide gate, not a shovel.
  5. 5. Watch three outlets continuously: CLEAN outlet (your product), LIGHT/ASPIRATION outlet (dust, chaff, husk - collect in a bag, it is saleable as cattle feed), and STONE/HEAVY outlet (stones, sand, mud balls - collect separately and check it daily for good grain loss).
  6. 6. Run the clean outlet over a MAGNET: either a magnetic grate fitted in the discharge chute, or - at micro scale - pass a strong rare-earth magnet wrapped in a plastic sleeve through the grain in the bin, then peel the sleeve off and inspect what stuck. Do this every batch and record what you find.
  7. 7. Sieve a 500 g sample on the target mesh to confirm sizing and check for remaining foreign matter. Weigh the foreign matter; it must be <=0.5%.
  8. 8. Second visual check: spread 500 g thinly on a white tray under good light. Look specifically for discoloured grains (grey, black, pink - these are mould or disease), and pull them out.
  9. 9. Weigh the cleaned grain. Record input weight, output weight and CLEANING LOSS %. Expected: ragi 1-2%, jowar 1-2%, bajra 1-2%, kuttu 2-4% (it is dirty), rajgira 3-6% (very sandy).
  10. 10. If the loss is far outside these ranges, either the grain was bad (talk to the supplier with the evidence) or your aspiration is set too high (fix it).
  11. 11. Bag the clean grain into clean, food-grade, labelled liners: 'CLEANED | <grain> | Lot <code> | Wt <kg> | Moisture <%> | Date/Time | Operator'.
  12. 12. Between two DIFFERENT grains, run 5 kg of the NEXT grain through and discard it as purge, or blow down and brush the machine. This is your cross-contamination control.
  13. 13. Empty and inspect the stone reject cup at the end of every run. A cup that is filling with good grain means your settings are wrong.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Output visually clean, foreign matter <=0.5%, no stones found in a 500 g white-tray check, loss in range
THEN PASS -> route per product: S04 (sprouted SKUs) or S06 (bajra raw) or S07 (everything else)
IF Chaff/dust/light grain still visible
THEN Increase aspiration one notch, re-run the batch. Re-check. Maximum 2 passes - more passes crack the grain.
IF STONES FOUND IN THE CLEAN OUTLET
THEN STOP. Quarantine the whole cleaned batch. Re-run it through the destoner. Then inspect the destoner: sieve wear, deck angle, vibration amplitude, feed rate. A destoner that lets stones through is the most dangerous machine in the plant.
IF Cleaning loss > 6% (or >3% for ragi/jowar/bajra)
THEN Investigate before continuing - you are either blowing good grain out of the aspirator, or the lot is far worse than the supplier declared. Record it and raise it with the supplier in writing.
IF Discoloured / mouldy grains found in the tray check (>2%)
THEN Reject the lot back to S02 intake QC. Do not clean and use.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Skipping destoning because 'the supplier says it is clean'
→ One stone = one steel fragment = one recall. Never skip.
✗ Aspiration set too high
→ You lose 3-5% good grain out of the dust outlet. Check the dust bag daily - if it is full of whole grains, turn it down.
✗ Feeding too fast
→ The bed on the destoner deck gets too deep and stones ride over the divide. Slow down - throughput is not your bottleneck.
✗ Not purging between grains
→ Ragi seeds inside your jowar pack. Customers photograph it.
✗ Worn sieve not replaced
→ Grading fails silently. Inspect sieves weekly; replace on the first sign of a hole or stretched mesh.
S04  —  Washing, Soaking & Germination (SPROUTING)  | FL-SPRAGI-03, FL-SPJOWAR-04 (and the sprouted components of MX-MALT-08 and MX-HEALTH-09) | 36-60 h per batch (ragi 36-48 h, jowar 48-60 h)
Purpose
Activate the grain's own enzymes: raise available iron and calcium, cut phytate (the anti-nutrient that blocks mineral absorption), build the malty flavour, and pre-soften the grain so it dries and mills better. This is the step that justifies a 2-3x price premium on your sprouted SKUs - and it is also your biggest food-safety risk.
Inputs
Cleaned ragi/jowar, potable (preferably RO/UV) water, food-grade soaking tanks, perforated germination trays, muslin cloth, sanitiser (sodium hypochlorite) + test strips, germination room with AC/dehumidifier, T-RH data logger, timers
Outputs
Uniformly sprouted grain, rootlet 0.5-2 mm, 80%+ germinated, sweet/fresh aroma, zero sourness or slime. Must go to S05 within 30 minutes.
Critical parameters
Soak: ragi 8-10 h / jowar 10-12 h at 25-30 C, water changed once | Germination: 25-28 C, 80-85% RH, dark | Rinse-turn-drain every 6-8 h | Stop: ragi 24-36 h (rootlet 0.5-1.5 mm, >=80%), jowar 36-48 h (rootlet 1-2 mm) | Sanitiser 200 ppm chlorine, verified by test strip | To dryer within 30 min
Automation level
MANUAL (90%) with AUTOMATED MONITORING (10%) - and the monitoring is the part worth automating
How to automate it
Do NOT buy an automatic sprouting machine at this scale - imported units run Rs 3-10 lakh, are designed for bean sprouts (not cereal grain), and are hard to service. The right automation here is CONTROL and RECORDING, not movement: (1) a Wi-Fi/GSM temperature-humidity data logger with SMS alerts (Rs 3,000-9,000) in the germination room and in the dryer; (2) a split AC + dehumidifier holding 25-28 C / 80-85% RH; (3) a dosing pump or a marked chlorine dosing jug + test strips so sanitiser strength is never guessed; (4) phone alarms every 6 h for the rinse cycle; (5) a printed laminated SOP card on the wall. Total cost of this 'smart' package: Rs 60,000-1,20,000 including the AC - versus Rs 3-10 lakh for a machine you would still have to babysit.
Machines / equipment
SS304 or food-grade HDPE soaking tank 100-200 L with a bottom drain valve (Rs 15-45k) | perforated HDPE germination trays 60x40x8 cm, 40-80 pcs (Rs 250-600 each) | SS trolley racks 5-8 tier (Rs 8-18k each) | split AC 1.5-2 ton + dehumidifier (Rs 45-90k) | T-RH data logger with alarm (Rs 3-9k) | chlorine test strips (Rs 600-1,500/100) | 20 L graduated dosing jug | muslin cloth
Manual work remaining
2 people per batch day, working in 2 shifts to cover the 6-8 hourly rinses. This is the most labour-intensive stage in the plant. Train them hardest here - this is where a food-safety disaster is born.
Quality checks
Every batch: appearance, aroma, rootlet length, % sprouted, grain temperature, rinse log, T-RH trace. Every batch of finished sprouted flour: full microbiological panel. Water: potability test monthly. Trays: ATP swab weekly once you scale.

Step by step

  1. 1. PLAN THE BATCH BACKWARDS. Sprouting takes 36-60 h total, so decide your DRYING day first, then work back. A 20 kg dry-grain batch becomes ~45-50 kg of wet sprouted grain - confirm your trays and dryer can hold it (see capacity maths in the Excel workbook).
  2. 2. SANITISE everything first. Soak tank, trays, muslin, scoops, trolley: wash with food-grade detergent, rinse, then sanitise with 200 ppm chlorine solution (make it by diluting household sodium hypochlorite 5.25% - roughly 4 ml per litre of water - and CONFIRM with chlorine test strips, do not guess). Contact 2 minutes, drain, air-dry. Do this every single batch.
  3. 3. Weigh the dry grain and record it. This is your yield denominator.
  4. 4. WASH: fill the tank, agitate vigorously by hand or paddle for 60 seconds, let it settle 1 minute, skim off everything that floats (floaters are hollow, insect-damaged or immature - they will never sprout and they will rot first). Drain. REPEAT 3 TIMES until the water runs clear.
  5. 5. Final rinse with potable water only (no chlorine) so no residue carries into the sprout.
  6. 6. SOAK: 1 part grain to 3 parts potable water. Cover the tank with a clean lid or mesh to keep insects out. Room temperature 25-30 C.
  7. - RAGI: soak 8-10 hours.
  8. - JOWAR: soak 10-12 hours (bigger, harder grain).
  9. 7. At the mid-point (hour 4 for ragi, hour 5 for jowar) drain and replace the water. Stagnant soak water goes sour and breeds bacteria; this one habit is the difference between a clean sprout and a smelly one.
  10. 8. If ambient temperature is above 32 C, shorten the soak by 1-2 hours or move the tank to a cooled room. Warm soak water ferments.
  11. 9. DRAIN COMPLETELY: lift the grain out on a mesh screen and let it drain 20-30 minutes. Water must STOP dripping. Free water in the tray = anaerobic pockets = sour, smelly, unsafe sprouts.
  12. 10. LOAD THE TRAYS: spread the grain 2-3 cm deep (never more - a deep layer heats up in the middle and rots). One tray per 4-6 kg of wet grain. Stack on a trolley rack with 8-10 cm between trays for airflow.
  13. 11. COVER with a clean, damp (not wet) muslin cloth. This holds humidity at the grain surface without sealing it.
  14. 12. GERMINATION ROOM: 25-28 C, 80-85% RH, no direct light, gentle air movement (a slow fan on oscillation, NOT blowing directly on the trays). Fit a continuous T-RH data logger with an alarm - if the room goes above 30 C at 3 am you must get an SMS.
  15. 13. RINSE + TURN + DRAIN every 6-8 hours (3-4 times a day, including one night shift - yes, someone must come in). Gently lift and turn the grain with clean hands or a clean paddle, mist with potable water if the surface looks dry, and make sure the tray drains fully. Turning stops the rootlets from matting into a solid cake.
  16. 14. INSPECT at 18 h, 24 h, 30 h, 36 h, 42 h, 48 h and record: % grains showing a white point, rootlet length in mm, aroma (fresh/sweet/sour/musty), grain temperature, and any slime.
  17. 15. STOP POINT: ragi at 24-36 h when rootlets are 0.5-1.5 mm and >=80% of grains show a white point. Jowar at 36-48 h when rootlets are 1-2 mm and the shoot just shows. Aroma must be fresh, sweet, like wet cereal - never sour, never alcoholic, never musty.
  18. 16. Do NOT let the rootlet exceed 2 mm. Beyond that the seedling consumes the sugars and proteins you are trying to sell, the flour turns bitter and fibrous, and your yield falls.
  19. 17. When the stop point is reached: give a final potable rinse, drain 15-20 minutes thoroughly, weigh (record wet weight for yield), and MOVE TO THE DRYER WITHIN 30 MINUTES. Wet sprouted grain held at room temperature for more than 1-2 hours starts to sour irreversibly.
  20. 18. Record the batch: lot code, dry weight in, soak start/end, germination start/end, room T and RH trace, every rinse time, operator initials, appearance at stop point, wet weight out.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF At the stop point: >=80% sprouted, rootlet 0.5-2 mm, fresh sweet aroma, grain temp <=28 C, no slime
THEN PASS -> go to S05 drying WITHIN 30 minutes
IF At 36 h only 50-79% sprouted, aroma still fresh, no slime
THEN EXTEND by 6-12 h, inspecting every 4 h. Record the extension. If it still fails, the GRAIN is the problem (old crop / poor germination capacity) - raise it with the supplier and use the batch only after full sensory and micro testing.
IF SLIME on grains, sour / alcoholic / putty smell, grey-green-black fuzzy patches, or grain temp >32 C
THEN FAIL - DESTROY THE ENTIRE BATCH. Do not wash it, do not dry it, do not 'pick out the bad trays'. Photograph it, log a Non-Conformance Report, destroy it in a way that it cannot re-enter the food chain (compost/denature), then: deep-clean and 200 ppm-sanitise the room, tanks, trays and muslin; re-test your water source; and find the root cause - almost always one of (a) non-potable water, (b) water pooling from poor draining, (c) layer too deep, (d) room too hot, (e) trays not sanitised, (f) rinses missed on the night shift.
IF Any batch that looked or smelled borderline but was dried anyway
THEN That dried batch is QUARANTINED and must be micro-tested (TPC, yeast & mould, coliform, E. coli, Salmonella, B. cereus) before release. No exceptions - and note that drying does NOT kill Salmonella.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Using bore-well or unchlorinated municipal water
→ The number-one cause of a sour or unsafe sprout. Use RO/UV water and test it monthly.
✗ Water pooling in the tray
→ Anaerobic, sour, slimy. Drain 20-30 min after soaking and after every rinse. Tilt the trays.
✗ Layer deeper than 3 cm
→ The centre heats to 35 C+ and rots while the top looks fine.
✗ Over-sprouting (rootlet >2 mm)
→ Bitter, low yield, fibrous. Set an alarm, and physically look at the grain - do not trust the clock alone.
✗ Missing the night rinse
→ 8 hours without a rinse at 28 C is enough to spoil a batch. Put it in the shift rota and the alarm system.
✗ Holding wet sprouted grain while you 'find dryer space'
→ It sours in 1-2 h. Book the dryer BEFORE you start the soak.
✗ Unsanitised trays reused
→ Batch 1 fine, batch 3 spoiled, and you cannot work out why. Sanitise every time and log it.
S05  —  Drying (Tray Dryer / Dehydrator)  | FL-SPRAGI-03, FL-SPJOWAR-04, MX-MALT-08 & MX-HEALTH-09 components, and any grain received at 12.6-14% moisture | 6-9 h per batch (sprouted grain); 1-2 h for moisture correction of dry grain
Purpose
Remove the water you added in S04 (and any excess from intake) using LOW heat, so you preserve the enzymes, vitamins, colour and flavour you paid for by sprouting - and so the grain is hard and stable enough to mill and store.
Inputs
Wet sprouted grain (45-50% moisture), tray dryer, moisture analyser, SS trays, muslin, IR thermometer
Outputs
Dried grain at 8-10% moisture, hard and snapping, colour unchanged, cool to touch, lot-coded and weighed
Critical parameters
Chamber 50-55 C (never >60 C for sprouted) | tray load <=2 cm depth | fan continuous, damper ~25% open | rotate trays every 2 h | end moisture 8-10% | snap test must pass | cool to <=32 C | total 6-9 h
Automation level
AUTOMATED (80%) - temperature, fan and timer are machine-controlled; loading, rotating and unloading are manual
How to automate it
12-24 tray SS304 electric tray dryer with digital PID controller, circulation fan and over-temperature cut-out. 12-tray (~12-25 kg wet load) Rs 35,000-90,000; 24-tray (~25-60 kg wet load) Rs 80,000-1,80,000. Insist on: SS304 trays AND chamber, a PID (not a bimetal thermostat), a separate over-temperature safety cut-out, and a door gasket that seals. Add a Rs 3-9k Wi-Fi data logger so you get an SMS if the chamber exceeds 62 C at night.
Machines / equipment
Tray dryer (Vidya Udyog Ambala / Universal Engineers Ghaziabad / Agroripe Pune / local SS fabricators) | halogen moisture analyser | IR thermometer | SS trays
Manual work remaining
1 operator, part-time - load, rotate every 2 h, unload, clean.
Quality checks
Moisture every 2 h during drying and at the end. Independent thermometer cross-check weekly. Snap test every tray-load.

Step by step

  1. 1. Preheat the dryer to 50 C for 20-30 minutes BEFORE loading. Loading into a cold dryer means the first hour is wasted and the grain sits wet and warm - exactly the window microbes love.
  2. 2. Surface-dry the sprouted grain first: spread on a clean SS mesh/perforated tray and blow a fan over it for 15-20 minutes. This removes free surface water and cuts drying time by 1-2 hours.
  3. 3. Load the trays at MAXIMUM 2 cm depth, evenly spread with a flat spatula. Overloading is the most common mistake and it silently doubles your drying time.
  4. 4. Set the profile: 50-55 C for the first 4-6 hours, then 55-60 C for the final 1-2 hours. NEVER exceed 60 C for sprouted grain - above that you inactivate the very enzymes and destroy the vitamins you sprouted to create, and the flour darkens.
  5. 5. Keep the circulation fan ON continuously and the exhaust damper about 25% open so moist air actually leaves the chamber. A closed damper just re-circulates humid air and the grain never dries.
  6. 6. Rotate the trays top-to-bottom and front-to-back every 2 hours. Every tray dryer has hot and cool spots; rotation is the fix.
  7. 7. CHECK MOISTURE every 2 hours: take ~20 g from 3 different trays, mix, and run the halogen moisture balance (2-3 min) OR use the oven method (105 C for 4 h, or 130-133 C for 2 h per FSSAI method). Record each reading.
  8. 8. Cross-check with the operator's physical test: bite a grain. It must be HARD and SNAP cleanly with a sharp crack. If it bends, feels chewy, or leaves a mark on your tooth, it is not done - moisture meters lie if they are not calibrated.
  9. 9. Stop at 8-10% moisture. Do NOT over-dry below 7%: you lose weight (= money), the grain becomes brittle and produces excess flour-dust at grinding, and the colour dulls.
  10. 10. Switch off the heaters but LEAVE THE FAN RUNNING for 15-20 minutes with the door closed. This equalises moisture between the grains - 'tempering' - and prevents a wet core.
  11. 11. Unload onto clean SS trays, cover with muslin, and cool to <=32 C. Weigh and record. Expected: 1 kg dry grain in -> 2.2-2.5 kg wet sprouted grain -> back to ~1.02-1.05 kg dried sprouted grain.
  12. 12. Label the container: lot code, product, moisture %, weight, date/time, operator. Move to S07 roasting while still slightly warm if you can - it saves energy.
  13. 13. Clean the dryer: brush out every tray, vacuum the floor and the fan intake, wipe the door gasket. Sprouted-grain residue left in a dryer grows mould overnight and contaminates tomorrow's batch.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Moisture 8-10%, grain snaps, colour unchanged, aroma sweet/cereal
THEN PASS -> S07 gentle roast (or S09 if going straight to grind)
IF Moisture 10-12%
THEN Continue drying at 55-60 C in 30-minute increments, re-checking each time. Record the extra time.
IF Moisture <7%
THEN Accept but note it: lower yield, more brittle grain, more dust at grinding. Next batch reduce drying time by 30-45 min.
IF Grain is browned, smells cooked/toasty/burnt, or the snap test passes but colour has darkened
THEN FAIL THAT TRAY. Quarantine it. Check the thermostat against an independent thermometer - a 10 C overshoot is the usual cause. Re-calibrate before the next batch. A whole-chamber failure means re-roast at a lower temperature or scrap.
IF Sour or musty smell after drying
THEN The sprout was already spoiled. QUARANTINE and micro-test. Do not 'roast it out' - roasting hides the smell but not the toxins.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Trays loaded 4-5 cm deep
→ Outside dry, centre wet. You measure 'dry' grain from the top and pack a wet centre. Max 2 cm.
✗ Drying above 65 C to 'save time'
→ You have just made ordinary flour and destroyed the reason this SKU costs double.
✗ No tray rotation
→ Trays near the heater over-dry and brown; trays at the back stay wet.
✗ Skipping the tempering/fan-only step
→ Uneven moisture inside the grain; the flour re-absorbs and cakes in the pouch.
✗ Not cleaning the dryer between batches
→ Mould spores from yesterday's residue land on today's batch.
S06  —  Dehusking / Dehulling & Polishing (OPTIONAL - bypass at micro scale)  | FL-BAJRA-05 (only if raw bajra is purchased). Kuttu and rajgira are ALWAYS bought dehusked at this scale. | 100-250 kg/h if installed
Purpose
Remove the inedible husk from bajra. Applies ONLY if you buy raw (un-dehusked) bajra.
Inputs
Cleaned raw bajra (12-13% moisture), millet dehuller/polisher, aspirator, weighing scale
Outputs
Dehusked, polished bajra kernels - husk <=2%, broken <=10%, clean and free-flowing
Critical parameters
Grain moisture 12.5-13.5% | dehusking efficiency >=90% | broken <=10% | recovery 75-80% | to roasting same day
Automation level
AUTOMATED (90%) if installed - but the recommended Phase-1 answer is OUTSOURCE THIS STEP
How to automate it
Single-stage or double-stage millet dehuller with polisher, 100-250 kg/h, 3-5 HP. Rs 1,50,000 - 2,30,000 (Nabhitha: millet dehuller Rs 1,85,000; meet-machines millet mill dehuller Rs 1,70,000; Perfura: single/double-stage dehullers). DEFER to Phase 2.
Machines / equipment
Millet dehuller cum polisher + aspirator (DEFER)
Manual work remaining
1 operator if installed; otherwise 0 - it becomes a purchase specification.
Quality checks
200-kernel dehusking count and broken count per batch. Yield % per batch.

Step by step

  1. 1. DECIDE FIRST whether to do this at all. Economics: raw bajra Rs 26-34/kg with 20-25% husk loss = effective Rs 36-45/kg of kernels. Dehusked bajra kernels cost Rs 52-70/kg. A dehuller costs Rs 1.5-2.3 lakh. Below ~150-200 kg/day of bajra, BUYING DEHUSKED KERNELS IS CHEAPER AND LOWER RISK. Do the arithmetic with your own quotes before spending money here.
  2. 2. If you proceed: CONDITION the grain to 12.5-13.5% moisture by misting 1-2% water and resting 10-15 minutes. Too dry and the kernel shatters; too wet and the husk turns to paste and blinds the machine.
  3. 3. Set the dehuller: choose the abrasive roll / emery cone clearance per the manufacturer's chart for bajra, and set the aspirator to a LOW setting first.
  4. 4. Run 2 kg as a trial. Inspect: is the husk off? are the kernels whole? is good grain going out with the husk?
  5. 5. Adjust in small steps: more husk left on -> tighten clearance slightly or slow the feed. Too many broken kernels -> loosen clearance, or raise moisture by 0.5%. Good grain in the husk outlet -> reduce aspiration.
  6. 6. Run production at the machine's rated feed (typically 100-250 kg/h), collecting dehusked kernels and husk separately. Bajra husk is excellent cattle feed - bag and sell it, it recovers 5-10% of your raw-material cost.
  7. 7. Polish (if the machine has a polisher head) to remove the remaining bran layer and give a bright, uniform grey-white kernel.
  8. 8. Grade and aspirate to remove loose husk, broken bits and dust.
  9. 9. CHECK: take 200 kernels, count those with husk still attached. Need >=90% fully dehusked. Count broken: need <=10%.
  10. 10. Weigh, record yield (expect 75-80% recovery from raw bajra), label, and move to S07 roasting IMMEDIATELY - dehusked bajra has lost its protective husk and starts oxidising the same day.
  11. 11. Never store dehusked bajra for more than 2-3 weeks. Buy raw, dehusk weekly.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF >=90% dehusked, <=10% broken, husk outlet contains no whole kernels
THEN PASS -> S07 roast within the same day
IF 70-89% dehusked
THEN Re-run once. Still low? Tighten the clearance one step and re-trial on 2 kg. Do not run a full batch on unverified settings.
IF Broken >10%
THEN Loosen the clearance, raise moisture to 13.5%, slow the feed. Broken bajra = flour with more free fat = faster rancidity.
IF Good kernels appearing in the husk outlet
THEN Reduce aspiration. Check the aspirator duct for a blockage.
IF BAJRA DECISION (Phase 1 recommendation)
THEN BYPASS S06 entirely - buy dehusked bajra kernels from an approved supplier, verify husk <=2% and no rancid smell at S02 intake, and go straight to S07. Install a dehuller only in Phase 2 when bajra volume exceeds ~150 kg/day.
IF KUTTU / RAJGIRA DECISION
THEN ALWAYS bypass S06. Small-scale buckwheat dehullers are not reliably available in India and amaranth is sold dehusked as standard. Buy 'kuttu dana' and 'rajgira seed'.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Buying a dehuller before you have the volume
→ Rs 2 lakh of idle iron. Outsource the step until bajra exceeds ~150 kg/day.
✗ Dehusking then storing for a month
→ Dehusked bajra oxidises fast. Roast the same day.
✗ Running at wrong moisture
→ Shattered kernels and a blinded machine.
S07  —  Roasting / Dry Heat Treatment ***THE MOST IMPORTANT STEP FOR SHELF LIFE***  | ALL 10 SKUs (temperatures differ - see product parameter table) | 15-35 min per batch + 15-20 min preheat; ~8-12 batches/day = 100-160 kg/day roasted capacity
Purpose
Inactivate lipase and other hydrolytic enzymes, drive moisture down to 3-6%, develop the roasted flavour, and reduce microbial load. Millet flours - BAJRA ESPECIALLY - go rancid in 10-15 days without this step. Roasting is what turns a 6-week product into a 6-9 month product, and it is the single biggest quality differentiator between your brand and an unbranded mandi flour.
Inputs
Cleaned / dried grain, drum roaster with temperature control, IR thermometer + dial thermometer, moisture analyser, cooling trays, timer
Outputs
Roasted grain at 3-6% moisture, correct colour and aroma for the SKU, fully enzyme-inactivated, lot-coded, with a recorded roast profile
Critical parameters
See the SKU table. Defaults: ragi 100-110 C/15-20 min | jowar 100-105 C/10-12 min | sprouted ragi & jowar 90-100 C/8-12 min | BAJRA 110-120 C/15-20 min (mandatory) | rajgira 85-95 C/4-6 min | kuttu 90-100 C/6-10 min. End moisture 3-6%. Grain temp verified by IR every 3-5 min. Batch size fixed per SKU.
Automation level
AUTOMATED (75%) - heating, drum rotation and temperature control are automatic; end-point judgement is human
How to automate it
Batch drum roaster, 10-25 kg per batch, SS304 food-contact drum, electric heating with digital PID temperature control and a thermocouple IN THE GRAIN BED (not just on the wall), variable drum speed, and a manual tilt discharge. 15 kg batch: Rs 85,000-1,50,000 (Nabhitha millet roaster ~Rs 87,925; Perfura drum roaster ~Rs 1,24,950; Mill Power/Pulverizer King roasting range Rs 70,000+). LPG-fired versions are ~30% cheaper to run but much harder to control - for a quality-first, low-labour unit choose ELECTRIC. Phase 2 upgrade: continuous roaster with a cooling conveyor, Rs 4-9 lakh.
Machines / equipment
Batch drum roaster 10-25 kg with PID + grain-bed thermocouple | IR thermometer (Rs 2-6k) | independent dial thermometer | retained colour standard jars (one per SKU) | white tile | halogen moisture analyser
Manual work remaining
1 operator for the whole roast cycle. He must NOT walk away - roasting is the step where a 5-minute distraction destroys a batch.
Quality checks
Colour vs standard, aroma, bite test, moisture, and a recorded temperature-time curve - every batch. Monthly controller calibration.

Step by step

  1. 1. READ THE ROAST TABLE for today's product before you switch anything on. Every SKU has a different temperature and time. Write the target on the batch card.
  2. 2. Preheat the drum for 15-20 minutes to the set point. Verify with an INDEPENDENT dial or IR thermometer, not just the machine's own display. Controller drift of 10-15 C is common on cheap machines and it is invisible unless you check.
  3. 3. Weigh the batch: 10-15 kg for ragi/jowar, max 10 kg for bajra, max 5 kg for rajgira, max 8 kg for kuttu. CONSISTENT BATCH SIZE IS ESSENTIAL - a 5 kg batch and a 20 kg batch in the same drum at the same temperature give completely different results.
  4. 4. Load, start the drum rotation (8-15 rpm) and start the timer.
  5. 5. Monitor grain temperature with an IR thermometer through the door/chute every 3-5 minutes and write it on the batch card. You are building a roast CURVE, and the curve - not the clock - is your real recipe.
  6. 6. Sensory checkpoints, in order, and how to read them:
  7. - Steam/aroma change: the first strong aroma means surface moisture is gone.
  8. - SOUND: grains crackle and pop while wet; the crackle gradually stops as they dry. Crackle stopping is your moisture cue.
  9. - COLOUR: pull 5-6 grains every 3 minutes onto a white tile and compare against a RETAINED COLOUR STANDARD jar for that SKU. Keep one jar per SKU on the shelf next to the roaster - this is the cheapest, most effective QC tool you will ever own.
  10. - SMELL: green/raw -> nutty/toasty -> chocolate/malt -> BURNING. Stop one stage before you think you need to; the grain keeps cooking for 3-4 minutes after discharge.
  11. - BITE TEST: at the expected end point, take 3 grains, let them cool 30 seconds, and bite. They must be CRISP and shatter, not bend or feel chewy.
  12. 7. Check moisture at the end point with the analyser: target 3-6% depending on SKU (bajra and rajgira <=4%).
  13. 8. DISCHARGE IMMEDIATELY at the end point onto perforated SS cooling trays. Do not let it sit in the hot drum 'for another minute'.
  14. 9. Record the full profile on the batch card: lot in, batch weight, set temperature, actual grain temperature every 5 min, total time, colour vs standard (pass/fail), aroma note, bite test, moisture out, weight out, operator. This record is what lets you reproduce a good batch and diagnose a bad one.
  15. 10. Move to S08 cooling. For bajra, cooling must start within 5 minutes.
  16. 11. Clean the drum after every product change: brush out, then run 1 kg of the next grain as a purge and discard it as 'roaster purge' (do not sell it).

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Colour matches the retained standard, aroma is correct for the SKU, bite test crisp, moisture 3-6%
THEN PASS -> S08 cooling immediately
IF Under-roasted: colour too light, aroma still green/raw, bite test chewy, moisture >6%
THEN Continue roasting in 2-minute increments, re-checking each time. Record the extra time and use it to correct the next batch's set point.
IF Over-roasted: darker than the standard, bitter or burnt smell, or any blackened grains
THEN FAIL. Quarantine the ENTIRE batch. Over-roasted flour cannot be blended away - it tastes burnt at any dilution. Segregate it (it can be sold as animal feed), log an NCR, check the thermocouple and controller calibration, verify the batch weight, and re-train the operator on the colour standard.
IF Uneven roast - some grains dark, some light, within the same batch
THEN Batch too large for the drum, drum speed too slow, or the grain was not uniformly dry going in. Reduce batch size by 30%, increase rpm, and check the pre-roast moisture spread.
IF BAJRA shelf-life validation gate
THEN Every new roast profile for bajra must be validated: make a trial batch, pack it in your real pouch with an O2 absorber, store half at room temperature and half at 40 C / 75% RH (accelerated), and test peroxide value + free fatty acid + a blind smell/taste at day 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120. Only lock the profile once day-120 PV is acceptable. Repeat this test annually.
IF Roaster temperature does not match the independent thermometer by more than +-5 C
THEN STOP the roaster. Recalibrate or replace the thermocouple. Do not run production on an unverified temperature.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Under-roasting to 'save time or colour'
→ Rancidity in month 3-4, and the customer who finds it never comes back. Bajra especially.
✗ Over-roasting
→ Burnt, bitter, dark flour. Reject the whole batch - it cannot be blended away.
✗ Not cooling fast enough before grinding
→ Condensation inside the sealed pouch = mould in 3-4 weeks. This defect shows up AFTER the sale.
✗ Variable batch size
→ Your 'recipe' is 20 minutes at 105 C, but 20 minutes means nothing if the batch is sometimes 5 kg and sometimes 20 kg.
✗ Trusting the machine display without an independent check
→ Thermocouples drift. A Rs 2,000 dial thermometer saves a Rs 40,000 batch.
✗ No retained colour standard
→ Two operators, two different 'golden brown'. Make one jar per SKU and hang it at the machine.
S08  —  Cooling / Tempering  | ALL SKUs that go through S05 or S07 | 15-40 min per batch
Purpose
Bring the roasted or dried grain down to <=35 C before it touches the mill or the pouch.
Inputs
Hot roasted/dried grain, perforated SS trays, trolley racks, filtered-air fan, IR thermometer, muslin
Outputs
Grain at <=35 C (target 30 C), moisture stable, covered, labelled, ready to grind within the same shift
Critical parameters
Target <=35 C (aim 30 C) | time <=40 min | layer <=5 cm | filtered air | 3-point IR reading logged | grind within 8 h
Automation level
MANUAL (70%) / low-cost automated monitoring (30%)
How to automate it
There is no 'cooling machine' worth buying at this scale. The right spend is: perforated SS trays (Rs 800-2,000 each), a trolley rack (Rs 8-15k), an axial fan with a filter (Rs 4-9k), an IR thermometer (Rs 2-6k), and - the highest-value item - a DEHUMIDIFIER for the grinding and packing room (Rs 25-60k for 24-50 L/day). Phase 2: a cooling conveyor with a fluidised bed, Rs 1.5-3 lakh, which also feeds the mill automatically.
Machines / equipment
Perforated SS trays | trolley rack | filtered axial fan | IR thermometer | room dehumidifier
Manual work remaining
1 operator, part-time (he can also be the grinding operator).
Quality checks
3-point IR temperature logged per batch. Ambient T and RH logged twice daily.

Step by step

  1. 1. Discharge the hot grain onto PERFORATED SS trays in a layer no thicker than 5 cm. A deep pile holds heat in the middle for hours.
  2. 2. Place the trays on a trolley rack in the cooling area, with 8-10 cm between trays.
  3. 3. Blow FILTERED air across the trays (an axial fan with a coarse filter on the intake, or the room's AC supply). Never blow unfiltered air from a dusty corridor onto open food.
  4. 4. Turn the grain once or twice with a clean SS paddle to expose the centre.
  5. 5. Measure with an IR thermometer at 3 points (top, middle of the pile, bottom) every 10 minutes. Log it.
  6. 6. Stop when all 3 points read <=35 C, ideally 30 C. Time required: 20-40 min for ragi/jowar, 15-20 min for rajgira/kuttu, and only 10-20 min for bajra (bajra must be cooled FASTEST).
  7. 7. Weigh and record any cooling loss (should be <=1%).
  8. 8. Transfer to a clean, closed, food-grade container with a lid. Label: lot code, product, weight, temperature at cooling, date/time, operator.
  9. 9. Cover with muslin whenever the container is open, and never leave cooling grain uncovered in a room where grinding or sweeping is happening.
  10. 10. Grind within the same shift - maximum 8 hours. Beyond that, moisture re-absorption starts.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF <=35 C at all 3 points
THEN PASS -> S09 grinding
IF 35-45 C
THEN Keep cooling, re-check in 10 minutes. Do not start the mill.
IF Room RH >70% while cooling
THEN The grain is re-absorbing moisture faster than it is cooling. Move the rack into the dehumidified grinding/packing room and finish there.
IF Grain has been cooling for >2 hours uncovered
THEN Moisture has risen and dust has settled. Re-check moisture; if >7%, return to S05 for a short drying pass; sieve before grinding regardless.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Grinding hot grain
→ Flour comes out at 55-65 C, packs 'sweat' inside the pouch, and mould appears in 3-4 weeks. Also the mill screens blind and the flour quality drops.
✗ Deep piles
→ Surface cool, centre hot. Spread it out.
✗ Unfiltered air in a dusty room
→ You are re-contaminating what you just roasted clean.
✗ Leaving it overnight uncovered
→ Moisture climbs 1-2%, insects land on it, and dust settles.
S09  —  Grinding / Pulverising  | ALL 10 SKUs (mesh differs - see product table) | 30-80 kg/h depending on mesh and grain
Purpose
Convert the roasted or dried grain into flour of a specified, repeatable particle size. Particle size decides mouthfeel, water absorption, how the roti/dosa behaves, and whether the customer calls your product 'premium' or 'gritty'.
Inputs
Cooled grain at <=35 C, pulveriser (and/or stone chakki) with the correct screen, clean food-grade bins, magnet, weighing scale
Outputs
Flour at the specified mesh, discharge temperature <=45 C, metal-free, lot-coded, weighed with yield recorded
Critical parameters
Mesh per SKU: ragi 60 | jowar 60 | sprouted ragi & jowar 80 | bajra 60 | rajgira 40-60 | kuttu 60 | malt & health mix components 80 | dosa mix 40-60 coarse + urad 80-100 fine (bimodal). Flour discharge temp <=45 C. Feed rate 20-40 kg/h per 5 HP. Motor load <=85%. Yield >=96%. Purge between products. Metal check every batch.
Automation level
AUTOMATED (85%) - the mill does the work; humans set it up, feed it steadily, and verify
How to automate it
PRIMARY: SS304 contact-part impact pulveriser / micro-pulveriser with cyclone + bag filter, 5-7.5 HP, 30-80 kg/h on millet flour, interchangeable screens (40/60/80/100 mesh), air-swept design so the flour is carried out by the blower (this keeps it cooler than a gravity-discharge mill). Budget Rs 90,000-1,80,000 for a 5-7.5 HP food-grade unit (Mill Power/Pulverizer King M3 3 HP ~Rs 22,800 entry, T10 10 HP ~Rs 1,04,600, M10 SS304 ~Rs 2,89,000; Nabhitha pulveriser ~Rs 2,25,038; Perfura single/double-stage pulverisers; Shreedhar double-stage). OPTIONAL SECONDARY: 2-3 HP stone chakki, 40-60 kg/h, Rs 25,000-55,000 - lower temperature, coarser flour, and a genuine 'stone-ground' marketing story. Cheap enough that owning both is worth it: the chakki is also your BACKUP if the pulveriser is down.
Machines / equipment
SS304 impact pulveriser 5-7.5 HP with cyclone + bag filter and interchangeable screens | optional 2-3 HP stone chakki | magnetic grate in the discharge chute | IR thermometer | IS test sieves 40/60/80/100 mesh | food-grade HDPE bins with lids | 100 kg scale
Manual work remaining
1 operator continuously while milling. 20-40 kg/h.
Quality checks
Sieve analysis every batch (weigh 100 g, sieve 5 min on a hand sieve or 10 min on a mechanical shaker, weigh the overs). Flour temperature every 10 min. Yield every batch. Magnet inspection every batch. Screen and beater inspection weekly.

Step by step

  1. 1. CHECK THE SETUP before every run - this is a 5-minute checklist that prevents 90% of grinding problems: (a) correct screen/mesh fitted for today's product, (b) screen intact with no holes, cracks or stretched mesh (hold it to the light), (c) beaters/hammers not worn below the limit and no missing beaters, (d) all contact parts clean, dry and free of the previous product, (e) gaskets and door seals in place, (f) cyclone and filter bag correctly fitted and empty, (g) magnet in the discharge chute, (h) collection bin clean, dry and labelled.
  2. 2. START-UP SEQUENCE: start the blower/cyclone FIRST, then the mill, then begin feeding. Stopping is the reverse - stop feeding, let the mill run empty for 60 seconds, then stop the mill, then the blower. Getting this backwards dumps unground grain into your flour.
  3. 3. PURGE: run 0.5-1 kg of today's grain through and collect it separately as 'purge flour'. It carries whatever residue the previous product left. Do not sell it as the current SKU - re-blend it into the correct product's next batch or use it for internal trials.
  4. 4. FEED at a STEADY, EVEN rate - 20-40 kg/h for a 5 HP pulveriser on millet flour. Use the hopper slide gate; never pour from a bucket in surges. Watch the ammeter (or listen to the motor): it should sit at 70-85% of rated load. Above 90% you are overfeeding and will choke the mill or burn the motor.
  5. 5. MONITOR FLOUR TEMPERATURE continuously: catch a handful at the discharge and read it with an IR thermometer every 10 minutes. Target <=45 C, ideally 38-42 C. If it climbs above 50 C: reduce the feed rate, check that the blower is pulling enough air, and if it is still hot, pause 15 minutes between batches. Hot flour = accelerated rancidity + condensation in the pouch.
  6. 6. CATCH THE FIRST-DISCHARGE SAMPLE in a clear glass jar for every batch and set it on the QC shelf as a visual reference next to the retained standard.
  7. 7. When the batch is done, run 1 kg of the NEXT product as a purge (or clean the mill if the next product is an allergen or a different family), then collect.
  8. 8. Weigh the flour, record yield. Expected 96-98% of the input weight. Below 95% means the filter bag is leaking, the cyclone is blowing fines out, or the mill is retaining product.
  9. 9. CHECK FOR METAL: pass the magnet through the flour, then inspect the screen and beaters for any fresh damage. Any bright metal particle = quarantine the batch and open the mill.
  10. 10. Close the collection bin with a lid IMMEDIATELY. Flour sitting open in a 60% RH room gains 1-2% moisture in an hour.
  11. 11. SPECIAL CASE - OILY GRAINS (rajgira, kuttu): feed at HALF the normal rate, grind in 2-minute bursts with 1-minute pauses, use the coarsest acceptable screen, and purge with 1 kg of dry jowar afterwards. If the flour starts to ball up or coat the beaters, stop, clean, and either coarsen the screen or blend 20% dry jowar in as a grinding carrier.
  12. 12. SPECIAL CASE - STONE CHAKKI (if you install one for a 'stone-ground' premium SKU): dress/true the stones every 150-250 hours of running (a 20-minute job with a dressing stone), check the gap setting for each grain, and note that output is 30-40% lower and coarser than a pulveriser. That is the point - it is a marketing feature, not a defect.
  13. 13. Clean the mill at the end of the shift: brush out the chamber, cyclone and pipe; remove and wash the screen; vacuum, do not sweep, to keep dust out of the air.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Mesh check: >=98% passes the target sieve (>=95% for rajgira), flour temp <=45 C, no metal, yield >=96%
THEN PASS -> S10 sifting
IF 90-97.9% passes the target sieve
THEN Re-mill ONLY the overs fraction and return it to the sifter. Do not re-mill the whole batch - you will over-grind the fines into starch damage and the flour will absorb too much water.
IF <90% passes
THEN STOP. Check the screen for a wrong mesh or a hole, check the beater wear, and reduce the feed rate. Re-run.
IF Flour temperature >50 C
THEN STOP feeding. Reduce feed rate by 50%, check the blower and filter bag for blockage, and let the mill idle for 5 minutes to cool. Then restart slower.
IF Metal particles found, or the screen shows fresh damage
THEN QUARANTINE the batch AND the previous batch. Open the mill, find the source, replace the part, pass everything through the magnet and a fine sieve, and log an NCR. If in doubt, discard.
IF Oily grain is pasting and coating the beaters
THEN STOP. Clean the chamber. Halve the feed rate, coarsen the screen one step, and consider the 20% jowar carrier method. Never force it - you will burn the motor.
IF Yield <95%
THEN Check the filter bag for holes and the cyclone for leaks before you accept the loss. A leaking bag is silently sending your finest, most valuable flour into the air.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Wrong mesh screen fitted
→ You will not notice until the customer complains the flour is gritty - or that the dosa does not crisp. Check the screen number physically at setup.
✗ Overfeeding
→ Choked mill, burnt motor, hot flour, inconsistent particle size. Steady and slow beats fast and stalled.
✗ Not purging between products
→ Ragi flour in your jowar pack. Visible, photographable, brand-damaging.
✗ Worn beaters or a holed screen
→ Metal fragments and coarse particles. Inspect weekly, replace on schedule - keep 2 spare screens and 1 spare beater set on the shelf.
✗ Open bins in a humid room
→ Flour gains 1-2% moisture in an hour. Lids on, always.
✗ Grinding all your SKUs in one continuous run without cleaning
→ Allergen and cross-contamination risk. Sequence: plain flours first, then sprouted, then mixes, then oily grains last, then a full clean.
S10  —  Sifting / Grading / Dressing  | ALL 10 SKUs | 30-150 kg/h
Purpose
Guarantee uniform particle size, remove oversize bran and any unground particle, and - critically - catch foreign material before it reaches the consumer. This is the step that makes your flour feel 'premium' between the fingers.
Inputs
Ground flour, vibro sifter with the correct mesh, SS bins, weighing scale, magnet
Outputs
Graded flour, >=98% through the target mesh, overs re-milled or discarded, foreign matter zero, lot-coded
Critical parameters
Feed 30-60 kg/h | overs 0.5-2% | >=98% through target mesh (95% for rajgira) | overs inspected every batch | magnet pass | yield recorded
Automation level
AUTOMATED (85%)
How to automate it
Vibro sifter / sifter-shaker, 24-30 inch (600-750 mm) diameter, single or double deck, SS304 food grade, 0.5-1 HP, 30-150 kg/h. Rs 35,000-90,000 (Shivansh Engineering Ahmedabad, Premium Engineering Faridabad, Mill Power ~Rs 83,200 for an SS304 unit, Perfura flour sifter). At micro scale you can start with a hand sieve + a mechanical sieve shaker (Rs 12-25k), but a vibro sifter pays for itself in 3 months on speed alone.
Machines / equipment
Vibro sifter SS304, 24-30 in, single/double deck | spare screens 40/60/80 mesh | magnetic grate | SS bins with lids | 100 kg scale
Manual work remaining
1 operator, part-time (can be shared with the grinding operator).
Quality checks
Overs % and overs INSPECTION every batch. Sieve analysis every batch. Mesh integrity check weekly.

Step by step

  1. 1. Fit the correct mesh screen for the SKU (60 for plain flours, 80 for sprouted and mixes, 40-60 for the dosa mix coarse fraction). Check the screen for damage and for residue from the last product.
  2. 2. Start the sifter, then feed slowly and evenly at 30-60 kg/h. Dumping a whole bin in at once overloads the deck, and the overs fraction escapes into the fines.
  3. 3. Collect two streams separately: FINES (your product) into a clean, labelled, lidded bin; OVERS/TAILINGS into a second labelled bin.
  4. 4. Weigh both. The overs fraction should be 0.5-2%. Calculate and record it.
  5. 5. INSPECT THE OVERS EVERY BATCH - do not skip this. Spread it on a white tray. It should be only coarse bran and endosperm bits. If you find stones, metal, plastic, jute fibre, insect parts or anything unrecognisable, STOP the line and go back to S09/S03 to find the source. The sifter's overs stream is your plant's early-warning system - it is telling you what got past the earlier controls.
  6. 6. Re-mill the overs ONCE through the pulveriser and return it to the sifter. If it is still overs after one re-mill, discard it (sell as cattle feed) - it is mostly bran and repeated milling just makes it hot and oxidised.
  7. 7. Pass the finished flour over the MAGNETIC GRATE one more time on the way into the bin.
  8. 8. Do a quick hand feel-and-look test: rub a pinch between clean dry fingers - it must be smooth with no grit; look at it on a white tile under good light - uniform colour, no specks.
  9. 9. Weigh the final flour, record the yield, label the bin (lot, product, weight, mesh, date/time, operator) and move it to S13 (packing) or S12 (blending).
  10. 10. Clean the sifter between products: remove the screen, brush both sides, vacuum the deck and the skirts, and check the gaskets. Sifters hide flour in the skirt seals, and hidden flour = insects in 3 weeks.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Overs <=2% and contains only bran/endosperm, flour smooth and uniform
THEN PASS -> S12 blending (mixes) or S13 metal detection (single flours)
IF Overs 2-5%
THEN Re-mill the overs once, re-sift, record. Investigate the mill screen and feed rate if it recurs.
IF Overs >5%
THEN STOP. The mill screen is wrong, holed, or you are overfeeding. Fix at S09 before continuing.
IF FOREIGN MATERIAL in the overs (stone, metal, plastic, jute, insect)
THEN STOP THE LINE. Quarantine the batch. Trace back: S03 cleaning failure? S09 mill wear? a broken tool? packaging from a raw material? Log an NCR with the physical evidence in a labelled bag. Do not restart until the source is identified.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Dumping the whole bin in at once
→ Overs escapes into the fines; the sifter does nothing.
✗ Not inspecting the overs
→ You throw away your only daily evidence of upstream failure.
✗ Re-milling the overs 3-4 times
→ Hot, oxidised, dark flour and a burnt smell. Once only, then discard.
✗ Skipping cleaning between products
→ Hidden flour in the skirt seals breeds insects and cross-contaminates.
S11  —  Ingredient Preparation & Staging for Ready Mixes  | MX-MALT-08, MX-HEALTH-09, MX-DOSA-10 | 60-90 min per blend batch
Purpose
Get every mix ingredient roasted, ground, sieved, weighed and staged BEFORE blending starts, so the blender is never waiting and no ingredient is missed.
Inputs
In-house flours (from S10), bought-in ingredients with COAs, roaster, pulveriser, sieves, calibrated platform scale, labelled staging bins, batch recipe card
Outputs
A fully staged, weighed, verified, labelled set of ingredients for one blend batch - 'mise en place'
Critical parameters
Recipe card signed | COA on file for every bought ingredient | calibrated scale verified daily with a standard weight | micro-ingredients (<2%) always geometrically diluted | second-person verification | allergens in red bins
Automation level
MANUAL (75%) with instrument support (25%)
How to automate it
The 'automation' here is a good scale and good paperwork, not a robot. Buy: a 150 kg x 5 g platform scale with a printer or RS232 output so the weight prints onto the batch card (Rs 8-20k), a 30 kg x 1 g bench scale for micro-ingredients (Rs 3-8k), and a set of calibrated standard weights for daily verification (Rs 3-8k). An Excel batch-record sheet with locked formulas and auto-calculated totals removes arithmetic errors for free. Phase 2: a semi-automatic auger dosing station with load-cell feedback (Rs 1.5-2.5 lakh) for the top 3 high-volume ingredients.
Machines / equipment
Platform scale 150 kg x 5 g (with print/RS232) | bench scale 30 kg x 1 g | calibrated standard weights | labelled SS/HDPE staging bins | red allergen bins | printed recipe cards
Manual work remaining
1-2 people. 60-90 minutes of staging for a 100 kg blend batch.
Quality checks
Scale verified daily with standard weights. Second-person verification signature on every ingredient. COA file complete.

Step by step

  1. 1. Print the BATCH RECIPE CARD for the SKU and the batch size. It lists every ingredient, its exact weight, its lot code space, and a sign-off box. No one blends from memory.
  2. 2. Verify every bought-in ingredient has: an FSSAI licence number on the pack, a batch/lot number, a best-before date that is comfortably ahead of your own best-before, and a Certificate of Analysis on file. No COA = do not use.
  3. 3. PRE-ROAST the ingredients that need it: green gram, chana dal, poha, groundnut, almond, gond, fennel - each separately in the drum roaster at 95-105 C for 6-10 min until aromatic and crisp. Cool to <=32 C. Record each one.
  4. IMPORTANT: do NOT roast the urad dal for the dosa mix (it must stay raw to foam) and do NOT re-roast the sprouted flours (you would destroy them).
  5. 4. GRIND each roasted ingredient separately to the required mesh. Nuts: 20-second bursts with 1 tablespoon of base flour as a carrier, or you get butter, not powder.
  6. 5. SIEVE everything through 30 mesh (600 micron) to break lumps and catch foreign matter. Jaggery powder especially - it lumps instantly in humidity.
  7. 6. WEIGH each ingredient separately on a calibrated platform scale (150 kg x 5 g, or 30 kg x 1 g for micro-ingredients). Put each into its own labelled staging bin. Write the actual weight on the recipe card.
  8. 7. GEOMETRIC DILUTION for every ingredient below 2% of the batch (salt, baking soda, citric acid, cardamom, dry ginger, cinnamon, mineral/vitamin premix). Method: weigh the micro-ingredient, mix it by hand with 10 times its weight of a base flour from the same recipe in a clean bowl until uniform; then mix THAT pre-blend into the rest. This is the only reliable way to get 800 g of baking soda evenly spread through 100 kg - without it you get yellow bitter 'soda spots' in a few dosas and a perfectly fine rest of the batch, which is the worst kind of defect because it is random.
  9. 8. SECOND-PERSON VERIFICATION: a second person re-weighs or verifies every ingredient >=1 kg and every micro-ingredient, and signs the card. This one habit catches almost all formulation errors, and formulation errors are the most expensive errors in a mix plant.
  10. 9. Allergens (groundnut, almond, milk powder) go into RED bins and are staged on a separate red-marked tray, physically apart, so they cannot be added by mistake or added twice.
  11. 10. Stage everything within arm's reach of the blender, covered, in the order it will be loaded.
  12. 11. Record on the card: batch number, SKU, batch size, each ingredient with lot code and actual weight, pre-roast profiles, grind mesh, the person who weighed and the person who verified, and the time staging was completed.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF All ingredients staged, weighed, verified and signed
THEN PASS -> S12 blending
IF An ingredient is short, out of spec, past its best-before, or has no COA
THEN STOP. Do not substitute silently. Either raise an emergency purchase, or the production planner formally re-sizes the batch and re-issues the recipe card. Never 'add a bit more of something else'.
IF A weighed ingredient is out by more than +-2% (or +-0.5% for micro-ingredients)
THEN Re-weigh. If it cannot be corrected, discard that ingredient and start again - do not top up a bin that already contains the wrong amount.
IF The mix contains an allergen and today's schedule has a nut-free batch after it
THEN Resequence: run nut-free FIRST, then the allergen batch, then a documented full wet-clean. Check the changeover SOP (S21) before starting.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Weighing by volume ('2 buckets of ragi flour')
→ Density changes with humidity and with how tightly it is packed. Your formulation silently drifts every day. Always weigh.
✗ Skipping geometric dilution for soda/salt/minerals
→ Random hot spots. A customer gets one terrible dosa and tells ten people.
✗ Substituting an ingredient without re-issuing the recipe card
→ The label no longer matches the pack. That is an FSSAI mislabelling violation, not a small thing.
