✗ Not verifying the scale
→ Every batch is wrong by the same unknown amount. Verify daily - it takes 60 seconds.
S12  —  Blending (Ribbon Blender)  | MX-MALT-08, MX-HEALTH-09, MX-DOSA-10 | 50 kg per 18-20 min cycle = ~120-150 kg/h
Purpose
Produce a homogeneous mix in which every 30 g serving has the same composition as every other serving.
Inputs
Staged, weighed, verified ingredients; ribbon blender SS304; clean, dry, tared discharge container
Outputs
Uniform blend, verified by a marker-assay across 5 sample points with RSD <=5%, lot-coded, weighed, sealed
Critical parameters
Cycle 10+3+5 min (mixes) / 8+2+4 min (dosa mix) | fill 60-75% of rated capacity | 5-point uniformity RSD <=5% | yield >=98% | clean immediately after discharge
Automation level
AUTOMATED (80%)
How to automate it
Ribbon blender, 50 kg per batch, SS304 U-trough with a full-length double ribbon, 2-3 HP, reversible drive (a VFD makes the reverse cycle effortless), a flush-bottom discharge valve, and a lid safety interlock. Rs 55,000-1,20,000 (Sarva Mangal Engineering ~Rs 56,500 for 50 kg SS304; Mill Power/Pulverizer King ribbon blender; Chamunda Industries from ~Rs 24,900 for smaller MS units - insist on SS304 for food). Buy 50 kg, not 25 kg - the price difference is small and you will grow into it. Phase 2: 100-200 kg with a load cell under the blender so it weighs as it blends (Rs 2.5-5 lakh).
Machines / equipment
Ribbon blender 50 kg SS304 with reversible drive and flush-bottom discharge | 5 sampling cups | salt/conductivity kit for the uniformity test | 100 kg scale
Manual work remaining
1 operator. 25-30 min per batch including loading, blending and discharge.
Quality checks
5-point uniformity RSD every batch (then every 5th). Yield every batch. Visual lump/streak check every batch.

Step by step

  1. 1. INSPECT the blender first: chamber clean and dry, no residue in the ribbon ends or the discharge valve, the discharge valve closes fully, the gasket is intact, the lid interlock works.
  2. 2. LOAD IN ORDER - this matters more than people think: (a) the largest-volume base flours first (about half of them), (b) the mid-volume ingredients (sugars, dal powders, poha), (c) the remaining base flour on top, (d) the geometrically-diluted pre-blends LAST, scattered across the top surface. Loading micro-ingredients first buries them at the bottom where the ribbon moves them least.
  3. 3. Close and latch the lid. Confirm the interlock engaged.
  4. 4. BLEND on a fixed, documented cycle: 10 minutes forward, 3 minutes reverse, 5 minutes forward = 18 minutes total for a 50 kg ribbon blender at 60-70% fill. Do not exceed 75% fill - an overfilled ribbon blender cannot convect and will leave unmixed pockets.
  5. 5. For the DOSA MIX specifically, use a SHORTER cycle: 8 min forward, 2 min reverse, 4 min forward. Its particle size is bimodal (coarse millet + fine urad), and long blending SEGREGATES it - the fines migrate to the bottom and the coarse fraction rises. Over-blending is the classic dosa-mix failure.
  6. 6. UNIFORMITY CHECK - do this on every batch until you have 20 consecutive passes, then every 5th batch: take 5 samples of 100 g each from (i) top-left, (ii) top-right, (iii) centre-depth, (iv) bottom-left near the discharge, (v) bottom-right. Test a MARKER in each: salt (easiest - dissolve 10 g of sample in 100 ml water, measure conductivity or titrate), or iron if you fortify, or the soda content. Calculate the mean and the relative standard deviation.
  7. 7. Target RSD <=5%. (For a 100 g sample of a well-mixed powder this is easily achievable; RSD >10% means grossly non-uniform.)
  8. 8. DISCHARGE into a clean, dry, tared, food-grade container with a lid. Weigh and record the yield. Expected yield 99-100% of the input; below 98% means material is being left in the ribbon ends or lost as dust.
  9. 9. Label the container: SKU, batch number, net weight, blend start/end time, uniformity RSD, operator, blender-verified-by.
  10. 10. Clean the blender IMMEDIATELY after discharge, before the residue sets: dry-brush, then wash with food-grade detergent, rinse, sanitise (200 ppm chlorine or 70% alcohol), air-dry, and leave the lid OPEN so the chamber dries completely. A closed damp blender grows mould overnight.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF RSD <=5%, yield >=98%, no visible lumps or streaks
THEN PASS -> S13 metal detection
IF RSD 5-10%
THEN Blend 5 more minutes and re-test at 5 points. If it now passes, record it and check whether the loading order or the fill level was wrong. Two consecutive failures = stop and investigate the blender.
IF RSD >10%
THEN QUARANTINE the batch. Causes, in order of likelihood: overfilled chamber, wrong loading order, ribbon worn or bent, discharge valve leaking material during blending, or a micro-ingredient that was not geometrically diluted. Fix the cause, re-blend once, re-test; if it still fails, the batch is re-worked by re-sifting and re-blending in two half-batches.
IF Lumps or streaks visible in the discharged blend
THEN Sieve the whole batch through 30 mesh and re-blend. Find out why - usually jaggery powder or milk powder that was not sieved at staging.
IF An ingredient was found to be missing or double-added after blending
THEN QUARANTINE. Assess: if the missing/doubled ingredient is a flavour spice at <1%, a documented risk assessment may allow release with a label check; if it is salt, soda, an allergen or a fortificant, the batch CANNOT be released. Destroy or downgrade it. This is why second-person verification at S11 exists.
IF Allergen batch just finished
THEN Do not start the next batch until the documented full wet-clean is complete and signed off (see S21 changeover SOP).

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Overfilling the blender to 100%
→ The ribbon cannot convect; you get a mixed shell and a raw core. Max 75%.
✗ Over-blending the dosa mix
→ Segregation, not mixing. Shorter is better for bimodal particle sizes.
✗ Skipping the uniformity test because 'it looks mixed'
→ It always looks mixed. Only an assay tells you the truth.
✗ Not cleaning the ribbon ends and discharge valve
→ Yesterday's allergen in today's nut-free pack.
S13  —  Foreign Material & Metal Control  | ALL 10 SKUs | No extra time in Phase 1 (in-line magnet). Phase 2 adds ~0 seconds (in-line detector) or 20-40 packs/min (conveyor).
Purpose
Last physical barrier before the pack. Remove or detect metal, and confirm no stone, plastic or insect fragment has survived S03/S09/S10. This is both a consumer-safety control and an FSSAI expectation.
Inputs
Flour or blend ready for packing; magnetic grate / rare-earth magnets; metal detector (Phase 2); 30 mesh sieve; reject log
Outputs
Product that has passed magnetic separation and (Phase 2) metal detection, with every alarm investigated and logged
Critical parameters
Magnet pull and inspection every 2 h | 30 mesh sieve before filling | Phase 2: Fe 1.5 mm / NFe 2.0 mm / SS 2.5 mm detection, tested every 2 h | every reject logged and investigated | no loose metal, glass or brittle plastic in the packing area
Automation level
PHASE 1: MANUAL (magnets + sieves). PHASE 2: AUTOMATED (metal detector)
How to automate it
Phase 1 spend: rare-earth magnetic grate or 2-3 sleeved magnets (Rs 2,500-12,000) + a 30 mesh hand sieve. That is it - do not skip this because it feels primitive; it is genuinely effective for ferrous metal from mill wear. Phase 2: gravity free-fall metal detector for powders, or a small conveyor metal detector for sealed pouches, Rs 2,50,000-6,00,000 installed (Indian makers: Nexgen Packtech, Garvens India, Mettler-Toledo/Sesotec channels, Sandeep Instrumentation, Sharpex; many Ahmedabad/Delhi packing-machine makers supply them as an add-on). Also budget a CHECKWEIGHTER (Rs 1.5-3 lakh) in Phase 2 to verify every pack's weight automatically - it pays for itself by cutting over-fill give-away from ~2% to ~0.4%.
Machines / equipment
Rare-earth magnetic grate / sleeved magnets | 30 mesh sieve | (Phase 2) free-fall or conveyor metal detector + checkweigher
Manual work remaining
1 person in the packing area, as part of the filler operator's role.
Quality checks
Magnet inspection every 2 h. Detector test cards every 2 h. Reject log reviewed weekly by the owner.

Step by step

  1. 1. PHASE 1 (from day one, low cost): fit a MAGNETIC GRATE or a sleeved rare-earth magnet (10,000+ gauss) in the flour chute between the sifter and the filler. Pull and inspect it at the start of the run, every 2 hours, and at the end. Wipe what you collect onto a white tissue, note it in the METAL/FMD LOG, and if it is more than a trace, stop and investigate the mill.
  2. 2. Sieve the product through 30 mesh immediately before filling - this is your last chance to catch a stone, a jute fibre or an insect.
  3. 3. Keep the filling area free of glass, brittle plastic, staples, paper clips, pens with caps, and loose tools. Use a shadow board for tools and count them in and out. A single staple in a pouch is a recall.
  4. 4. PHASE 2 (at ~150 kg/day or when you supply a modern-trade retailer, who will demand it): install a metal detector - either a gravity free-fall head on the flour chute or a small conveyor unit that inspects sealed pouches.
  5. 5. If a metal detector is fitted, TEST IT with certified test cards/pieces - ferrous 1.5 mm, non-ferrous 2.0 mm, stainless 2.5 mm - at the START of the run, EVERY 2 HOURS, at every product changeover, and at the END of the run. Record every test with a pass.
  6. 6. On ANY reject: isolate that pack and everything produced since the last successful test, log the time, batch, product and what triggered it, then sieve/open the rejected pack to find and identify the contaminant. Photograph it. Bag and label it as evidence. Investigate the source (mill screen, beater, sieve frame, a tool, a supplier's raw material). Write an NCR. Only re-run the isolated product after the cause is fixed.
  7. 7. If a test card FAILS to be detected, the detector is out of specification: stop, quarantine all product back to the last passing test, and call for service. Do not 'run it and see'.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Magnet clean or trace-only, sieve clean, (detector passes all 3 test cards and no rejects)
THEN PASS -> S14 filling
IF Detector fails a test card
THEN STOP THE LINE. Quarantine all product since the last passing test. Re-test after service/recalibration; re-run the quarantined product through the detector. Log the downtime and the cause.
IF A pack is rejected by the detector, OR visible metal is found on the magnet beyond trace
THEN Isolate, sieve, identify, photograph, log, investigate to root cause, write an NCR. Do not release the isolated product until the cause is closed.
IF Stone, glass, plastic or insect fragment found in the sieve tailings
THEN STOP. Trace back to S03 (cleaning), S10 (sifting) or a raw material. Quarantine the batch. If it is glass or hard plastic, discard the batch - these are not recoverable risks.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ No magnet fitted because 'the mill is new'
→ New mills shed the most metal in their first 200 hours. Fit it on day one.
✗ Detector installed but never tested with cards
→ Worse than no detector - it gives false confidence and fails every audit.
✗ Rejects thrown away without investigation
→ You will never find the source, and it will keep happening.
✗ Loose tools, staples or a glass bulb in the packing room
→ The most common source of physical contamination in small units. Shadow board, no glass policy, plastic-covered lights.
S14  —  Weighing & Filling  | ALL 10 SKUs | 200-500 pouches/h (semi-auto); 100-180/h (manual)
Purpose
Put the right amount of product into every pack - legally compliant (never short), consistent, fast, and without giving away margin through over-filling. A 2% average over-fill on 500 g packs is Rs 10 per kg of pure lost profit.
Inputs
Sifted flour or verified blend, pouches/bags, weighing filler or scale + scoop, dehumidified packing room, daily scale calibration weights
Outputs
Filled, open pouches at the target weight, checked every 30 minutes, with the daily weight record signed
Critical parameters
Room <=25 C / <=55% RH | scale calibrated daily with a standard weight | filler verified with 5 test pouches at start | target = declared + 0.4% | SD <=1% of nominal | absolute minimum per pack = declared - 1.8% | 5-pouch check every 30 min | powder level >=25 mm below the seal area | O2 absorber count reconciled
Automation level
AUTOMATED (70%) with manual pouch handling
How to automate it
RECOMMENDED DAY-ONE MACHINE: semi-automatic LOAD-CELL BASED AUGER FILLER / weigh-filler with a foot pedal, range 10-2000 g, +-0.5-1% accuracy, SS304 contact parts, 200-500 packs/h. Rs 65,000-2,25,000 (Genius Engineering & Solutions / GES Packaging, Faridabad lists a semi-automatic load-cell auger filler at ~Rs 2,25,000; many Ahmedabad, Delhi and Coimbatore makers supply 10-1000 g units at Rs 65,000-1,40,000 - get 3 quotes and DEMAND a live demo with YOUR flour). BUDGET ALTERNATIVE (works fine below ~300 packs/day): a good 30 kg x 1 g digital bench scale + a calibrated scoop + a weigh-and-top-up routine. Rs 4-9k. Slower and more dependent on operator discipline, but honest. PHASE 2: automatic VFFS (vertical form-fill-seal) pouch packing machine with a servo auger, 20-60 pouches/min, Rs 3,80,000-8,80,000, which forms the pouch from roll stock, fills and seals in one action and adds a date coder inline. Only worth it above ~2,000 packs/day of a single SKU.
Machines / equipment
Semi-auto load-cell auger filler (10-2000 g) | 30 kg x 1 g bench scale | certified standard weights (500 g, 1 kg, 2 kg) | pouch magazine/rack | O2 absorber count tray | room dehumidifier + T-RH logger
Manual work remaining
1 operator per filling station, 200-500 pouches/h with a semi-auto filler; 100-180/h by hand with a scale.
Quality checks
Daily scale calibration record | 5-pouch weight check every 30 min | O2 absorber reconciliation | room T-RH log

Step by step

  1. 1. PREPARE THE ROOM: packing must happen in a separate room from grinding, at <=25 C and <=55% RH, with the dehumidifier running. Check and log the T-RH before you start. Above 60% RH, STOP - flour gains moisture in the pouch and caking starts.
  2. 2. CALIBRATE THE SCALE daily, before the first fill: place the certified standard weight (e.g. 500 g) and confirm the reading is within +-1 g. Record it. Do this every single day - it takes 60 seconds and it is the difference between legal compliance and a Legal Metrology fine.
  3. 3. VERIFY THE FILLER: run 5 test pouches at the target weight, weigh each on the verified bench scale, and record mean and spread. Only start production when the mean is at or just above the target and the spread is tight.
  4. 4. Set the filler's target weight to the SKU's TARGET (not the declared weight): 500 g pack -> set 502 g; 250 g -> 251.5 g; 1 kg -> 1003 g; 400 g -> 402 g. This 'plus' covers the legal requirement that no pack is short.
  5. 5. Hold the pouch open under the fill nozzle (or place it on the filler platform), trigger with the foot pedal, and let the filler complete its coarse-then-fine (dribble) cycle. Do not pull the pouch away early.
  6. 6. Tap or settle the pouch gently ONCE to drop the product, then check the powder level is at least 25-30 mm BELOW the seal area. Powder in the seal zone is the number-one cause of leaking seals.
  7. 7. If the SKU requires it, drop in the OXYGEN ABSORBER sachet now (mandatory for bajra and rajgira, recommended for sprouted and nut-containing mixes). Count them out on a tray so you can prove none is missing - a missing absorber is invisible later, and a double absorber is a choking hazard in a food pack. Log absorbers issued vs packs sealed at the end of the run; the numbers must match.
  8. 8. WEIGH EVERY 10th POUCH on the verified bench scale during the run, and do a full 5-pouch check every 30 MINUTES. Record all of them on the FILLING WEIGHT CHART with the time and operator initials.
  9. 9. If the mean drifts below the target, adjust the filler set-point UP by 1-2 g, then re-check 10 pouches before continuing.
  10. 10. If the spread widens (some packs 495 g, some 512 g), STOP and find out why: auger wear, load-cell drift, product density change (freshly ground flour is fluffier than flour that has settled), operator pulling the pouch away early, or a draft blowing on the scale. Fix it - a wide spread means you either go illegal on the low side or lose margin on the high side.
  11. 11. Keep the filling bin COVERED between pouches. Do not leave 20 kg of flour open in the packing room over lunch.
  12. 12. At the end of the run: count the pouches filled, reconcile against the oxygen-absorber count and the product consumed, record the total, and clean the filler (brush, vacuum, wipe - do NOT wash an auger filler with water unless it is designed for it).

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Mean >= declared weight, SD <=1%, no pack below declared - 1.8%, room RH <=55%
THEN PASS -> S15 sealing
IF Mean below target but above declared - 1.8%
THEN Adjust the filler set-point up by 1-2 g, re-check 10 pouches, continue. Record the adjustment.
IF ANY pack below the absolute legal minimum
THEN Remove it from the line, top it up and re-weigh, or scrap it. Then immediately investigate - check the last 20 packs. If more than one is short, quarantine the whole run since the last good check and 100% re-weigh it. Under-weight packs are a Legal Metrology offence.
IF SD >1.5%
THEN STOP filling. Calibrate/check the load cell, inspect the auger for wear, confirm the product density has not changed, retrain the operator's rhythm. Do not resume until 10 consecutive pouches are within +-1%.
IF Room RH >60%
THEN STOP filling. Run the dehumidifier until RH <=55%. Any flour that has been sitting open for more than 1 hour must be re-sieved and re-checked for moisture before it is used.
IF Powder visible in the seal area
THEN Brush or blow it out before sealing; if it is widespread, reduce the fill level, clean the nozzle, and check for a leaking filler chute.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ No daily calibration
→ Your weights drift silently and you either go illegal or give away 3% margin.
✗ Filling to exactly 500 g
→ Half your packs will be under 500 g. Always set 502 g.
✗ Over-filling to 510 g 'to be safe'
→ That is Rs 20/kg of product you are giving away. On 50 kg/day that is Rs 30,000/month. Tune the machine instead.
✗ Powder in the seal area
→ Leaks. The most common packing complaint in small units.
✗ Humid packing room
→ Caking, clumping, mould, and short shelf life - all discovered by the customer, not by you.
✗ Oxygen absorbers issued but not reconciled
→ Some packs will have none and you will never know which.
S15  —  Sealing & Pouch Closing  | ALL 10 SKUs | 400-900 pouches/h
Purpose
Create a hermetic, tamper-evident, moisture- and oxygen-barrier seal that survives transport and keeps the product dry for the full shelf life.
Inputs
Filled pouches, continuous band sealer, seal-test kit (squeeze + water/dye), lint-free cloth or brush, spare Teflon tape and heating element
Outputs
Sealed packs with a uniform 10-15 mm seal above the zipper, passing a squeeze test every 20th pack and a water/dye test every hour
Critical parameters
Temperature 150-170 C (film dependent) | speed 8-12 m/min | seal width 10-15 mm | seal above the zipper | visual 100% | squeeze test every 20th pack | water/dye test hourly | spare Teflon tape and element on site
Automation level
AUTOMATED (75%) - the sealer does the work; the operator feeds, inspects and tests
How to automate it
FR-900 series continuous band sealer (horizontal or vertical orientation depending on pouch weight), MS or SS body, digital temperature control, adjustable belt speed, with an optional embossing wheel for a simple batch code and an optional counter. Rs 11,000-22,000 for MS; Rs 25,000-45,000 for a heavy-duty SS body with printing. (Axeon Corporation, Sangli - FR900S ~Rs 20,000, vertical heavy duty ~Rs 22,000; also Crown Packaging Ahmedabad, Multi Packaging, Genuine Packaging Solutions Delhi, GES Faridabad, and every packing-machine dealer in India stocks them.) Choose the VERTICAL orientation for 1 kg+ bags and the HORIZONTAL for 200-500 g pouches; better still, buy one of each later. Add a small hand IMPULSE SEALER (Rs 2,500-6,000) for zipper ends and sample bags. PHASE 2 premium option: a band sealer with NITROGEN FLUSHING (Rs 55,000-1,20,000) - for bajra and rajgira this is a genuine shelf-life upgrade and a strong claim on the label.
Machines / equipment
FR-900 continuous band sealer (SS body preferred) | hand impulse sealer | spare Teflon tape, heating element, silicone rubber, belt | seal-test kit | (Phase 2) nitrogen flush attachment + N2 cylinder
Manual work remaining
1 operator, 400-900 pouches/h depending on pouch size and rhythm.
Quality checks
Visual 100% | squeeze every 20th | water/dye hourly and after every adjustment | sealer temperature logged at start and end

Step by step

  1. 1. SET THE SEALER: temperature 150-170 C for PET/AL/PE laminates (start at 155 C), belt speed 8-12 m/min, seal wheel pressure medium. The exact number depends on your film's total thickness - do a test seal on an empty pouch first and tear it open: a good seal shows FIBRE TEAR (the layers delaminate and rip) rather than peeling apart cleanly.
  2. 2. Clean the seal zone: brush or blow out any powder from the top 25-30 mm inside of the pouch. Powder in the seal = a microscopic channel = a leak. If your filler leaves powder consistently, fix the filler (S14 step 6) rather than fighting it here.
  3. 3. For ZIPPER pouches: seal ABOVE the zipper, and make sure the zipper is closed before sealing so the top of the pouch is flat. Also press the two ends of the zipper track to seal them (a small hand impulse sealer for 2 seconds does this) so the zipper does't leak at its ends.
  4. 4. Feed the pouch into the sealer belt with the seal area flat, unwrinkled, and square to the belt. Hold it until the belt grips it - let go too early and the pouch folds.
  5. 5. INSPECT EVERY SEAL VISUALLY: uniform width 10-15 mm, continuous, no wrinkles, no folds, no burnt or melted patches, no channels, and no product trapped in it.
  6. 6. SQUEEZE TEST every 20th pack: hold the pack with both hands and press firmly. The pack should bulge and hold; if it hisses or powder appears, the seal has failed.
  7. 7. WATER / DYE PENETRATION TEST every hour (and after every adjustment): take one sealed pack, fill it with air or a little water plus a drop of methylene blue, seal, and squeeze it under water looking for a stream of bubbles - or press a tissue against the outside of the seal while squeezing and look for a wet/dyed spot. Record the result.
  8. 8. If a seal fails: increase the temperature by 5 C, or reduce the belt speed, then re-test 5 packs. If the seal is melted, wrinkled or shiny, REDUCE the temperature by 5-10 C. If two adjustments do not fix it, STOP, quarantine everything sealed since the last passing test, and check the Teflon tape, the heating element and the silicone rubber for wear.
  9. 9. Count and record: packs sealed, packs rejected for seal failure, sealer temperature at start and end, and the hourly test results.
  10. 10. At the end of the run: let the sealer cool with the belt running (this prevents the belt from setting in a kink), then clean the belt, replace worn Teflon tape, and keep a spare kit (Teflon tape, heating element, silicone rubber, belt) on the shelf. The FR-900 series is a global standard and its spares are cheap and available everywhere - this is exactly why it is the right first machine.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Visual pass, squeeze pass, hourly water/dye pass, seal width 10-15 mm
THEN PASS -> S16 batch coding
IF Seal leaks on the squeeze test
THEN Increase temperature 5 C or reduce speed; re-test 5 packs. Quarantine everything since the last passing test until 5 consecutive packs pass.
IF Seal is melted / wrinkled / shiny / brittle
THEN Reduce temperature 5-10 C. Check the Teflon tape for damage and the silicone rubber for hardening.
IF Persistent failure after 2 adjustments
THEN STOP. Check: worn Teflon tape, failed heating element, uneven roller pressure, wrong film (a single-layer PE pouch will not seal at laminate temperatures), or powder contamination. Quarantine back to the last good hourly test.
IF Pouch is a zipper type and the zipper ends are not sealed
THEN Add the 2-second impulse seal at both zipper ends. An unsealed zipper end leaks slowly and the customer finds a stale product with no obvious defect - the worst kind of complaint.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Powder in the seal area
→ Leaks. Fix the fill height and clean the pouch top.
✗ Wrong temperature for the film
→ Either it does not seal (too cold) or it melts and wrinkles (too hot). Always test-seal a new film batch - suppliers change film grades silently.
✗ Worn Teflon tape
→ Sticky, torn, uneven seals. It is a Rs 100 consumable; change it the moment it discolours.
✗ Sealing below the zipper
→ The customer cannot close the pack and it leaks. Train it explicitly and put a photo of a correct seal at the station.
✗ No hourly seal test
→ You discover 3,000 leaking packs from customer complaints instead of from your own test.
S16  —  Batch Coding, Labelling & Legal Metrology Compliance  | ALL 10 SKUs | Inline with sealing
Purpose
Make every pack legally complete and traceable. The batch code is the difference between a surgical one-batch recall and a brand-killing total recall.
Inputs
Sealed packs, handheld TIJ inkjet printer or pre-printed labels, approved label artwork, batch-code generator, best-before calculator
Outputs
100% of packs carrying a legible, indelible batch code, MFG date, best-before date, MRP, and a fully FSSAI-compliant label
Critical parameters
Batch code format fixed | best-before per SKU table | first-print rub test passed | 5 packs checked hourly | all 13 label elements present | MRP never stickered over | no disease claims
Automation level
AUTOMATED (60%) - printing is automated; artwork control and verification are human
How to automate it
Handheld TIJ (thermal inkjet) batch coder: Rs 9,000-25,000 (BizBein, Sonic Industries, Axeon Corporation, and many IndiaMART suppliers; cartridges Rs 3,500-6,500 for 42-50 ml, which prints ~30,000-60,000 characters). Compact TIJ + conveyor inline setup: ~Rs 30,000. Inline CIJ (continuous inkjet) for Phase 2: Rs 1.2-3 lakh. Cheapest reliable route at start-up: pre-print the fixed artwork on the pouch (rotogravure/flexo from a pouch printer, MOQ 5,000-20,000 pcs) and TIJ-print only the VARIABLE fields (batch, MFG, best-before, MRP if it changes). Lowest-cost start: blank pouches + printed paper labels (MOQ 500) + TIJ for the variable fields. Design/label compliance: get your artwork checked ONCE by a food-regulatory consultant (Rs 5,000-15,000 per SKU) - far cheaper than a reprint of 20,000 pouches.
Machines / equipment
Handheld TIJ batch coder + cartridges | pre-printed pouches or printed labels | approved artwork file with version control | label applicator (optional, Rs 25-60k)
Manual work remaining
1 person, part-time; coding runs alongside sealing at 400-900 packs/h.
Quality checks
First-print verification + rub test | 5 packs hourly | label artwork version control | monthly traceability test

Step by step

  1. 1. FIX YOUR BATCH CODE FORMAT and never change it: <SKU>-<YYMMDD>-<LINE>-<SHIFT>-<SEQ>. Example: SPRAGI-260926-L1-A-003. Printed on the pouch AND written on the carton AND entered in the batch record. From a batch code alone, anyone must be able to find the grain lot, the roast profile, the operator and the customer.
  2. 2. CALCULATE the best-before date from the SKU table (9 months plain flours, 6 months sprouted and mixes, 4 months bajra, 6 months kuttu roasted / 3 months raw). Write it on the batch card BEFORE the run starts, so no one is doing date arithmetic at 6 pm.
  3. 3. Print with a handheld TIJ thermal inkjet printer using FOOD-GRADE SOLVENT-BASED ink (ethanol/MEK based, not water-based - water-based ink rubs off foil laminates). Print on the flat area of the pouch, not across a fold or a gusset.
  4. 4. VERIFY THE FIRST PRINT of the run: legible, correct dates, correct MRP, and it must PASS THE RUB TEST - rub hard with a dry thumb for 10 seconds, then with a damp tissue. If it smudges, change the ink or the printer setting before you print 2,000 packs.
  5. 5. Check 5 packs every hour for legibility, correct date, and print position.
  6. 6. LABEL CONTENT CHECKLIST - verify against the actual artwork at every reprint, because regulations and your own licence number change:
  7. a. Product name (as per FSSAI - e.g. 'Ragi Flour / Finger Millet Flour').
  8. b. List of ingredients in DESCENDING order of weight (single-ingredient flours may state the one ingredient).
  9. c. Net quantity in metric units, in the minimum font size prescribed by Legal Metrology for that pack size, in the specified position.
  10. d. MRP inclusive of all taxes. NEVER cover or alter a printed MRP with a sticker - that is a Legal Metrology violation.
  11. e. Month & year of manufacture ('MFG') and Best Before ('BEST BEFORE ... / use by').
  12. f. Batch / Lot / Code number.
  13. g. FSSAI logo and your 14-digit licence/registration number.
  14. h. Name and complete address of the manufacturer/marketer, plus customer-care contact and email.
  15. i. Nutrition Information panel per 100 g AND per serving, plus % RDA based on a 2,000 kcal diet.
  16. j. Vegetarian mark (green circle with a green dot in a square).
  17. k. Allergen declaration in BOLD ('Contains: Almond, Groundnut, Milk solids' or 'Processed in a facility that also handles nuts, milk and soy').
  18. l. Storage instructions ('Store in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and consume within 60 days.').
  19. m. Country of origin ('Product of India').
  20. n. If the pack is a jar/tub and not a pouch: still all of the above.
  21. o. 'Not intended as the sole source of nutrition for infants' - print this on the sprouted and malt SKUs.
  22. 7. CLAIMS DISCIPLINE: you may state factual nutrient content ('source of calcium', 'high in fibre') if you have a lab report supporting it. You may NOT claim to prevent, treat or cure any disease ('good for diabetes', 'cures anaemia'), and you may not use words like 'healthy' as a disease claim. Health/nutrition claims are regulated separately by FSSAI and by the ASCI code - getting this wrong is a real fine, not a warning.
  23. 8. Keep an approved ARTWORK FILE with the version number and the date it was approved, and destroy obsolete artwork plates/labels so old labels can never be used by mistake.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF All mandatory declarations present, legible, indelible and correct; batch code traceable end-to-end
THEN PASS -> S17 final QC
IF Any mandatory declaration missing, wrong, or printed in a non-permanent ink
THEN HOLD THE ENTIRE LOT. Re-label with a compliant printed label (you may over-label other information, but NEVER cover the MRP or the FSSAI number with a sticker). If over-labelling is not possible, the lot is repacked.
IF Batch code traceability test fails (cannot go from a pack to the grain lot, or from a grain lot to all packs, within 30 minutes)
THEN Stop shipping. Fix the records system before the next run. Run the traceability test monthly, not only when something goes wrong.
IF Best-before date calculated incorrectly
THEN Recall the affected packs from the finished-goods store before dispatch; if already dispatched, log it and assess a market recall with your FSSAI Designated Officer.
IF A health or disease claim appears on the artwork
THEN Do not print. Get it removed and re-approved. This is the most common way a new brand gets an FSSAI notice.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Water-based ink on a foil laminate
→ Rubs off in the customer's hand. Use solvent/ethanol-based food-grade ink.
✗ No best-before date, or a wrong one
→ An FSSAI finding and a customer complaint.
✗ MRP covered with a sticker
→ Legal Metrology violation - a fine, not a warning.
✗ Wrong or missing FSSAI number
→ Product is technically illegal to sell. Check the artwork against your actual licence certificate every time.
✗ Disease claims on the pack ('controls diabetes')
→ The fastest route to an FSSAI notice and an ASCI complaint.
✗ Using an old label version after a recipe change
→ Mislabelling. Destroy obsolete artwork.
S17  —  Final QC, Batch Release & Retention Samples  | ALL 10 SKUs | 20-30 min per batch (does not stop the line)
Purpose
The last gate. Nothing leaves the building until a named person has signed that it meets specification - and until you have kept evidence (retention samples) to defend yourself if a complaint arrives in month 5.
Inputs
Sealed, coded packs; moisture analyser; test sieves; sensory panel (2 people minimum); finished-goods QC report form; retention sample jars
Outputs
A signed batch-release record + 3 retention samples per batch + a released batch moved to finished-goods storage
Critical parameters
3 random packs per batch | moisture per SKU spec | particle size per spec | sensory scored and written down | weight stats from the fill chart | retention samples for shelf life + 3 months | named release signature
Automation level
MANUAL (85%) - this is judgement work, and that is exactly why it should be a human with a checklist
How to automate it
Instruments, not automation: halogen moisture analyser (Rs 18,000-55,000), IS test sieves + a mechanical sieve shaker (Rs 15,000-35,000), a 0.01 g analytical balance (Rs 12,000-30,000), retention-sample jars, and a laminated sensory score card. Phase 2: a checkweigher in-line (Rs 1.5-3 lakh), a camera-based label inspection system (Rs 2-5 lakh), and a cloud LIMS/QMS (Rs 500-2,500 per user per month) so records cannot be lost or back-dated. FREE TOOL WORTH USING NOW: an Excel QC workbook with locked formulas, drop-down pass/fail, and conditional formatting that refuses to print a release certificate unless every field is filled.
Machines / equipment
Halogen moisture analyser | IS test sieves + shaker | analytical balance 0.01 g | sensory score cards | retention sample jars | printed QC report forms
Manual work remaining
1 QC person, 20-30 min per batch including a cooking test for the dosa mix.
Quality checks
This stage IS the QC. Plus: monthly verification of the moisture analyser with a certified standard, and quarterly sieve calibration.

Step by step

  1. 1. VISUAL 100% check as packs come off the sealer: seal intact and uniform, label correct and legible, pouch clean (no powder on the outside), correct net quantity printed, no dents/leaks, zipper closed.
  2. 2. Pull 3 RANDOM packs from the batch (start, middle, end of the run) and open them for the lab check.
  3. 3. TEST: moisture (must meet the SKU spec - <=9% flours, <=6% mixes with milk/jaggery/nuts, <=7% bajra/rajgira/kuttu); particle size by sieve; and a full SENSORY evaluation.
  4. 4. SENSORY (train 2-3 people to do this consistently, and write down what you smell, do not just say 'OK'): appearance and colour uniformity against the retained standard; aroma - must be characteristic and fresh, with NO rancid/oily/painty/cardboard/sour/musty notes; texture by rubbing between the fingers - smooth, no grit; and a TASTE test - for flours, make a small slurry with warm water and taste it; for the malt mix, make the drink as the customer would; for the dosa mix, ACTUALLY MAKE A DOSA. You cannot release a dosa mix without cooking it.
  5. 5. Check weight compliance from the S14 filling chart: mean >= declared, no pack below the legal minimum, SD within limit.
  6. 6. Check the seal-test records from S15 and the metal/magnet records from S13 for this batch.
  7. 7. Complete the FINISHED-GOODS QC REPORT: batch code, SKU, quantity, moisture, particle size, sensory scores, weight stats, seal tests, metal check, any deviation and its disposition, tested-by, approved-by, date/time.
  8. 8. QA RELEASE SIGN-OFF: one named person (the owner at start-up, later a QA in-charge) signs 'RELEASED'. Until that signature exists, the batch is physically in a 'HOLD' area, not in finished-goods stock. Make the hold area a real, taped-off space - visual control beats paperwork.
  9. 9. RETENTION SAMPLES: put 3 unopened packs of every batch into labelled jars/boxes (batch code, SKU, MFG, best-before) and store them for the full shelf life PLUS 3 MONTHS. Store one set at room temperature and, if you can, one set at 40 C / 75% RH as an accelerated indicator. This is your evidence when a customer says 'it smelled funny' in month 6 - you can open your own retained pack and know instantly whether it was your product or their storage.
  10. 10. Record the batch in the FINISHED-GOODS REGISTER and move it to S18.
  11. 11. If any check fails, follow the decision gate below. Never 'release with a note'.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF All parameters within spec, sensory clean, records complete
THEN RELEASE -> S18 finished-goods storage
IF Moisture marginally above spec (e.g. 9.4% vs <=9.0%) with everything else fine
THEN HOLD. Re-sieve and re-dry the loose flour if it is not yet packed, or re-pack. If already packed, quarantine the batch, run an accelerated shelf-life check, and decide with a documented risk assessment - or downgrade it to a short-shelf-life 'fresh batch' for immediate local sale with a 6-week best-before. Do not ship a 9-month claim on a wet batch.
IF Particle size out of spec
THEN Re-sift (for coarse) or re-mill and re-sift (for fine). Re-test. If it cannot be corrected, downgrade it to a lower-value use - never to a customer-facing pack.
IF ANY off-odour (rancid, sour, musty, chemical) or off-taste
THEN QUARANTINE AND DO NOT RELEASE. Investigate: under-roasting? wet grain? contaminated store? old raw material? a dirty mill? Send a sample to the lab for peroxide value / free fatty acid / microbial. Over-roasted or rancid flour cannot be blended away.
IF Foreign material, insect, or metal found in a pack
THEN STOP SHIPPING THE ENTIRE BATCH. 100% inspect or destroy. Raise an NCR, find the root cause, and if any packs have already been dispatched, trigger the recall procedure (S20).
IF Weight or seal non-compliance
THEN 100% re-weigh or re-seal the batch, then re-inspect and re-release.
IF Records incomplete (no fill chart, no roast profile, no seal test)
THEN The batch is NOT releasable even if the product is perfect. Complete the records from contemporaneous notes, and fix the discipline problem. In an audit, an undocumented batch is a failed batch.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Shipping without a signed release
→ You lose the ability to say 'we checked'. One signature per batch costs nothing.
✗ No retention samples
→ Six months later a complaint arrives and you have no way to prove your product was fine. Rs 200 of jars saves your brand.
✗ Not cooking the dosa mix
→ You will ship a mix that does not crisp and blame the customer.
✗ Moisture testing only 'sometimes'
→ In the monsoon your flour can go from 8% to 11% in a week. Test every batch, and every day in June-September.
✗ Sensory testing by one person who has been in the room all day
→ Olfactory fatigue. Step outside for 5 minutes, use 2 people, and always compare against a retained standard.
S18  —  Cartoning, Finished-Goods Storage & FIFO  | ALL 10 SKUs | Not a bottleneck
Purpose
Protect the packs from light, moisture, crushing and pests, and make sure the OLDEST stock ships first.
Inputs
Sealed and released packs, 5-layer corrugated cartons, inner liner, carton labels, packing tape, pallets, racking, T-RH logger
Outputs
Sealed, labelled, palletised cartons in a finished-goods store at <=30 C / <=60% RH, with FIFO enforced and a dispatch-ready stock list
Critical parameters
5-layer cartons for shipped goods | 20-24 packs per carton, upright and interlocked | H-taped | full carton label | FG register updated same day | store <=30 C, <=60% RH | FIFO by best-before date | weekly stock and pest check
Automation level
MANUAL (90%)
How to automate it
Not worth automating at this scale. Spend instead on: pallets and boltless racking (Rs 15,000-60,000), a carton taping gun (Rs 800-2,000), a T-RH data logger with alarm (Rs 3,000-9,000), and an industrial dehumidifier (Rs 25,000-70,000) if your store is humid. Phase 2: a semi-automatic carton sealer (Rs 60,000-1,50,000) and a barcode/QR scanner linked to a stock sheet (Rs 8,000-25,000 + software) for real FIFO control.
Machines / equipment
Cartons and liners | taping gun | pallets and racking | carton label printer or pre-printed labels | T-RH logger | dehumidifier | hand pallet truck (Rs 12-25k)
Manual work remaining
1 helper. 20-30 min per 25-carton batch.
Quality checks
Weekly stock and pest check | T-RH twice daily | FG register reconciled weekly | near-expiry flag at 60 days

Step by step

  1. 1. Use 5-layer (double-wall) corrugated cartons for anything that will be couriered or stacked; 3-layer is fine only for direct local hand-delivery. Check the carton is clean, dry, odour-free and never previously used for chemicals.
  2. 2. Line the carton with a food-grade LDPE liner or a clean kraft liner if you are shipping in the monsoon.
  3. 3. Pack 20-24 x 500 g pouches or 40-48 x 250 g pouches per carton. Stand them UPRIGHT and interlock the layers - do not lay flat stacks on top of each other, the bottom pouches crease and the seals split.
  4. 4. Do not overfill the carton; a bulging carton bursts its tape in transit. Do not underfill either - a half-empty carton collapses when stacked.
  5. 5. Seal with 50 mm BOPP tape in an H pattern on both the top and the bottom.
  6. 6. LABEL THE CARTON with: SKU name and code, batch number, number of packs and total net weight, MFG date, best-before date, gross weight, 'Store in a cool dry place / Keep away from sunlight' and handling symbols (fragile is not needed, 'this way up' is), plus your company name and address.
  7. 7. Enter the carton into the FINISHED-GOODS REGISTER: batch code, SKU, cartons, packs, net weight, date, rack location.
  8. 8. Place in the FINISHED-GOODS STORE - a separate, dedicated area or room. NEVER in the raw-grain store and never next to it.
  9. 9. Storage rules: on pallets or racking, 15 cm off the floor, 45 cm off the walls, 60 cm aisles; cartons stacked max 5-6 high; away from direct sunlight and away from any water pipe, drain or roof leak; room <=30 C and <=60% RH (target 55%). Log T-RH twice daily.
  10. 10. ENFORCE FIFO physically: label each rack location with the batch's best-before date in large numbers, and arrange so the earliest date is at the picking face. A 'pick from here' arrow on the rack removes all ambiguity for a new helper.
  11. 11. Do a WEEKLY stock check: count cartons against the register, look for any damaged, leaking, infested or expired carton, and check for pest activity (droppings, webbing, live insects on the pallets).
  12. 12. Quarantine and destroy (or return to supplier) any carton found damaged, wet or infested - immediately, and away from good stock.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Carton sealed and labelled, register updated, placed in the FG store at the correct rack location, T-RH within spec
THEN READY FOR DISPATCH -> S19
IF FG store RH >60%
THEN Run the dehumidifier, find and fix the source (roof leak, open door, monsoon air, a wet floor), and inspect the bottom-layer cartons for softening. If pouches feel soft or the flour has caked, pull them for S17 re-inspection.
IF Damaged, leaking, crushed or infested carton found
THEN Remove it from the store immediately, open and inspect the packs, and either re-pack (with a new batch code suffix) or destroy. Investigate how it happened - stacking height? forklift? pests? Record it.
IF Stock approaching best-before (within 60 days)
THEN Flag it on the stock list and move it: discount to a fast-moving channel (a bakery, a hostel, a local kirana), or use it in your own trials. Never let it expire in your store - that is pure cash burnt.
IF More than 30 days of finished stock of a slow SKU
THEN Stop making it. Switch to make-to-order for that SKU. Millet flour is not a stock-and-wait product; freshness is your advantage.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Finished goods stored with raw grain
→ Insects migrate. This single mistake ruins stock and fails every audit. Separate them.
✗ No FIFO
→ You ship the newest batch while the oldest expires. Date-mark the rack faces, not just the cartons.
✗ Stacked 10 cartons high
→ Crushed bottom-layer pouches, split seals, customer complaints about leaking packs.
✗ Sunlight on the store wall/rack
→ Foil pouches protect the product, but heat and light still accelerate fat oxidation. Shade the store.
S19  —  Dispatch & Distribution Handover  | ALL 10 SKUs | Not a bottleneck
Purpose
Get the product to the customer in the same condition it left your QC bench.
Inputs
Released cartons, dispatch list, invoices, courier/transport partner, seal ties, dispatch register
Outputs
Dispatched orders with a complete record of batch codes, quantities, dates and customer contacts
Critical parameters
FIFO enforced | second-person pick verification above 10 cartons | minimum remaining shelf life per channel (>=60-70%) | complete customer contact record | same-day register update
Automation level
MANUAL (85%) - with cheap digital assistance
How to automate it
Barcode or QR labels on cartons scanned at dispatch into a Google Sheet / Excel with a linked batch-customer table (cost: a Rs 3,000-8,000 scanner and free software). Phase 2: a billing + inventory package (Busy, Marg, Tally, or a cloud D2C order-management system) that ties invoice -> batch -> customer automatically.
Machines / equipment
Barcode/QR scanner | carton labels | stretch wrap | dispatch register (Excel) | hand pallet truck
Manual work remaining
1 person, part-time.
Quality checks
Pick verification signature | dispatch register completeness audited weekly

Step by step

  1. 1. Pick strictly by FIFO from the rack face marked 'PICK HERE'.
  2. 2. Verify the pick against the order: SKU, batch code, carton count, pack count, best-before date. A second person signs the pick list for any order above 10 cartons.
  3. 3. CHECK THE BEST-BEFORE DATE against the customer's requirement. Most modern-trade retailers and quick-commerce platforms reject stock with less than 60-70% of shelf life remaining. Know your channel's rule and refuse to ship short-dated stock to a channel that will return it.
  4. 4. Palletise or bag the cartons, and wrap/stretch-wrap for courier shipments. For courier, put the carton inside a second carton or use a heavy-duty courier bag - single 5-layer cartons get punctured by other parcels.
  5. 5. RECORD THE DISPATCH: invoice number, date, customer name and FULL CONTACT DETAILS (phone, email, address), SKU, batch codes, carton and pack quantities, best-before, vehicle/courier AWB number, and the person who dispatched. Without the customer's contact details a recall is impossible.
  6. 6. Give the transporter written handling instructions: no stacking above X cartons, no exposure to sun or rain, no carrying alongside chemicals, detergents or fuel.
  7. 7. In summer, avoid leaving loaded vehicles standing in the sun; in the monsoon, tarpaulin everything and check for leaks before dispatch.
  8. 8. Update the FINISHED-GOODS REGISTER and the batch-to-customer TRACEABILITY sheet the same day - not at the weekend.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Pick verified, records complete, packaging adequate for the channel
THEN DISPATCH
IF Remaining shelf life below the channel's minimum
THEN Do not ship to that channel. Redirect to a faster-moving channel (local kirana, your own D2C, a bakery) or hold for the next order.
IF Wrong batch picked
THEN Return it to the rack, re-pick, and record the near-miss. Near-misses logged are errors prevented.
IF Customer contact details missing or illegible
THEN Do not dispatch until corrected. This is the field that makes a recall possible.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Dispatch records without customer contact details
→ You cannot recall what you cannot find.
✗ Shipping short-dated stock to a demanding channel
→ Returns, penalties, and a damaged trade relationship.
✗ Updating the register weekly instead of daily
→ Traceability becomes a reconstruction exercise instead of a lookup.
S20  —  Traceability, Complaint Handling & Recall Readiness  | ALL 10 SKUs - this is a system, not a step on the line | Mock recall 2 h, twice a year
Purpose
Make every pack traceable to a grain lot and every grain lot traceable forward to every pack - so a problem costs you one batch, not your brand. Also: know exactly what to do in the first hour of a real complaint.
Inputs
All batch records (RM register, sprouting log, roast profile, grind/sift record, blend card, fill chart, seal test, QC release, FG register, dispatch register), a written recall plan, the FSSAI Designated Officer's contact
Outputs
A working one-step-forward / one-step-back traceability system, tested twice a year, plus a documented complaint and recall procedure
Critical parameters
Mock recall every 6 months | traceability complete in <2 h | >=95% of dispatched quantity located | 100% complaint log closure | retention sample opened for every quality complaint
Automation level
MANUAL SYSTEM (70%) with spreadsheet automation (30%)
How to automate it
At this scale, a well-built Excel/Google-Sheets workbook with 3 linked tables and VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP is genuinely sufficient and costs nothing. Add QR codes printed on each carton (free generators + a Rs 3,000 scanner) so the lookup is instant. Phase 2: a cloud QMS/LIMS or an ERP with batch genealogy (Rs 30,000-1,50,000 per year). Do NOT buy software before you have run the paper system for 3 months - you will buy the wrong one.
Machines / equipment
Excel/Google Sheets batch-genealogy workbook | QR/barcode labels | complaint log | printed recall plan on the wall
Manual work remaining
Owner, 2 hours every 6 months for the mock recall; 15 minutes per complaint.
Quality checks
Mock recall report | complaint log review monthly | retention sample store audited quarterly

Step by step

  1. 1. Build a BATCH GENEALOGY sheet - three linked Excel tables: (Table 1) Raw material lot -> (Table 2) Process batch (with all parameters and operators) -> (Table 3) Finished batch code -> customer/dispatch. Link them by the lot and batch codes. Test that a VLOOKUP goes both ways.
  2. 2. Keep the physical batch card with each production run and file it by date. Paper + Excel beats an expensive system you never fill in.
  3. 3. WRITE A ONE-PAGE RECALL PLAN and stick it on the wall: who decides (the owner), who is called (FSSAI Designated Officer, your local Food Safety Officer, the lab, the customer), the timeline (isolate stock within 2 hours, notify the regulator and the customer within 24 hours), what to isolate (finished stock, in-transit stock, retained samples, all records), how to communicate (a written notice to every customer who received the batch, with the batch code and the reason), and how to close it (root cause, corrective action, effectiveness check, records filed).
  4. 4. Identify your FSSAI DESIGNATED OFFICER and Food Safety Officer contact details NOW, before you need them, and save them in your phone and on the wall.
  5. 5. RUN A MOCK RECALL EVERY 6 MONTHS: pick a random raw-material lot and trace it FORWARD to every finished batch and every customer; then pick a random finished batch code and trace it BACKWARD to the grain lot, the sprouting log, the roast profile and the operators. Time yourself. Target: complete in under 2 hours with >=95% of the dispatched quantity accounted for.
  6. 6. Document the mock recall: date, item chosen, time taken, % recovered, gaps found, actions with owners and due dates. Retest the gaps within a month.
  7. 7. COMPLAINT LOG: record every complaint with date received, customer, batch code, SKU, complaint description, photographs, quantity affected, where the pack was in the distribution chain, your investigation, the retention-sample result, the decision (replace / refund / recall / no fault found), and closure date. Review the log monthly - look for patterns by batch, by SKU, by season and by operator.
  8. 8. ALWAYS open your retention sample when a complaint mentions smell, taste, insects or caking. That single act tells you whether the fault was yours or theirs, and it is the reason you kept it.
  9. 9. Mandatory reporting: if you identify a product that is unsafe, notify the FSSAI Designated Officer immediately and initiate withdrawal under Section 28 of the FSS Act. Do not wait to 'see how many complaints come in'.
  10. 10. Review the whole system annually and after any near-miss.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Mock recall completed in <2 h with >=95% traceability and no critical gaps
THEN SYSTEM OK - file the report and retest in 6 months
IF Mock recall takes >2 h or finds gaps
THEN Identify each gap (missing customer contact, illegible batch code, a run without a batch card, register not updated) and assign an owner and a due date within 7 days. Retest that specific path within a month.
IF A real complaint indicates a SAFETY issue (metal, glass, insect infestation, off-odour across multiple packs, illness)
THEN TRIGGER THE RECALL PLAN IMMEDIATELY. Isolate all stock of that batch in the FG store within 2 hours. Notify the FSSAI Designated Officer and every customer who received that batch within 24 hours. Send the retention sample and a market sample to the lab. Do not ship anything else from that process batch until the cause is known.
IF A single complaint with a clean retention sample and no pattern
THEN Log it, replace or refund as a goodwill gesture, and monitor. Three similar complaints in 30 days = treat it as a systemic issue and investigate properly.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Never running a mock recall
→ You discover the gaps during a real crisis, when the clock is running and a regulator is on the phone.
✗ Batch codes that are not on the carton as well as the pouch
→ You cannot identify stock in a distributor's godown without opening cartons.
✗ Complaints handled by phone and never logged
→ You cannot see the pattern until the tenth complaint.
✗ No retention samples
→ You cannot prove your innocence.
S21  —  Cleaning, Sanitation & Pest Control (runs continuously, not once)  | ALL areas, every day | 30-45 min/day; 2-3 h/week
Purpose
Keep the plant in a state where an FSSAI inspector, a retail buyer's auditor, or a customer with a camera finds nothing to photograph.
Inputs
Food-grade detergent, sodium hypochlorite + test strips, 70% alcohol, brushes (colour-coded), vacuums, mops, pest-control contract, cleaning log
Outputs
A documented, verified clean plant with zero pest activity
Critical parameters
Daily 30-45 min | weekly 2-3 h strip-clean | monthly store and overhead clean | quarterly water and calibration | pest traps checked weekly, contractor monthly | colour-coded tools | chemicals locked and separate | waste out daily | cleaning verified and signed
Automation level
MANUAL (95%)
How to automate it
There is no machine for this at your scale - and that is normal. Worth buying: a wet/dry industrial vacuum (Rs 12,000-30,000) which is dramatically better than sweeping for flour dust; a high-pressure washer (Rs 8,000-20,000) for floors; colour-coded brush sets (Rs 3,000-6,000); chlorine test strips (Rs 600-1,500/100); a UV torch (Rs 800-2,500); and - when you scale - ATP hygiene swabs and a reader (reader Rs 40,000-90,000, swabs Rs 250-400 each). Phase 2/3 only: CIP for a closed system, which you do not have and do not need.
Machines / equipment
Industrial wet/dry vacuum | pressure washer | colour-coded brushes and mops | 3-sink wash station | chlorine test strips | UV torch | numbered pest traps and bait-station map | locked chemical cupboard
Manual work remaining
Everyone. 30-45 min daily by the shift team; 2-3 h weekly by 2 people.
Quality checks
Signed daily cleaning log | weekly white-glove/UV check | weekly pest-trap log | monthly contractor report | ATP swabs weekly once scaled

Step by step

  1. 1. DAILY - END OF SHIFT (30-45 min, non-negotiable): switch off and lock out all machines; brush down every machine and the floor (BRUSH AND VACUUM - do not dry-sweep, it puts flour dust into the air and into every open surface); wash all food-contact parts that are removable (screens, trays, bins, scoops) in the 3-sink method - (i) brush off dry soil, (ii) wash in warm water with food-grade detergent at the maker's dilution, (iii) rinse in clean potable water; then SANITISE with 200 ppm chlorine for 2 minutes contact, or spray 70% food-grade alcohol and air-dry (alcohol is better for electrical parts and for the packing room because it leaves no residue and no moisture); wipe all work surfaces, handles, switches and door handles; mop the floor with detergent and let it dry; empty all bins and take the waste OUT of the building; check that no product or open bag has been left uncovered.
  2. 2. WEEKLY (2-3 h): full strip-clean of the pulveriser (chamber, beaters, cyclone, pipe, filter bag), the vibro sifter (screen, deck, skirt seals - flour hides in the seals and turns into insects), the destoner (all sieves, aspiration duct, stone cup), the roaster drum interior, the blender (ribbon ends, discharge valve, lid gasket), the band sealer (belt, Teflon tape, rollers), the dryer (trays, chamber floor, fan intake, door gasket); clean behind and under every machine; wash walls and ledges within splash range; clean the fan filters and AC filters; inspect all sieves and screens for damage; check all magnets for collected metal and log it.
  3. 3. MONTHLY: full store clean-out - move every pallet, sweep and mop under it, inspect for pests and moisture; clean the roof/beams/light fittings for dust (a dust fall into open flour is an instant FSSAI finding); descale and calibrate the moisture analyser and the temperature controllers; inspect all hoses, gaskets, belts and electrical cords; deep-clean the sprouting room and sanitise every tray; service the dehumidifier.
  4. 4. QUARTERLY: inspect and clean the water tank and verify water potability by lab test; clean the exhaust ducts and fan blades; check all machine fasteners and guards; re-verify all scales against certified weights.
  5. 5. PEST CONTROL - the three-layer approach: (a) EXCLUDE - air curtain or PVC strip curtains at every external door, all doors and windows close-fitting with no gaps >6 mm, drain covers meshed, no vegetation or scrap within 2 m of the building, no wooden pallets in the packing room (plastic or steel only); (b) MONITOR - glue traps and pheromone traps for stored-product insects (flour beetle, Indian meal moth) placed along walls and under racks, numbered and mapped, checked WEEKLY and logged with the count; rodent bait stations OUTSIDE the building only, numbered, mapped, checked weekly by a licensed contractor - NEVER loose rodenticide inside a food building; a UV fly killer positioned away from open product and away from doors; (c) CONTROL - a licensed pest-control contractor on a MONTHLY visit with a written service report and a chemical list; you must keep their FSSAI-compatible pesticide list and confirm nothing is applied over open food.
  6. 6. COLOUR-CODE your cleaning tools and never cross them: RED = raw grain areas and floors; BLUE = processing machines; GREEN = packing room and food-contact surfaces; YELLOW = sprouting room (wet area); WHITE = QC bench. A floor brush in the packing room is a contamination event, not a shortcut.
  7. 7. CHEMICALS: store all detergents, sanitisers and pesticides in a locked cupboard, physically separate from food and packaging, in their original labelled containers, with a list on the door and an MSDS file. Only food-grade (FSSAI/IS-compliant) detergents and sanitisers inside the plant.
  8. 8. WASTE: covered, foot-operated bins, emptied at least daily and always before they overflow; waste removed from the building the same day; rejected/destroyed product denatured (dyed or mixed with waste) so it cannot re-enter the food chain, and its disposal logged with quantity and reason.
  9. 9. VERIFY: a supervisor signs the cleaning log daily; once a week do a WHITE-GLOVE / UV check - run a clean white cloth over a 'cleaned' surface, or use a UV torch to find organic residue. Better still, once you scale, use ATP swabs (Rs 250-400 each) on 5 points weekly and record the RLU values.
  10. 10. Keep the CLEANING LOG, PEST LOG and CHEMICAL REGISTER on a clipboard at the door and in the record file. These three logs are the first thing an auditor asks for.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Cleaning log complete and signed, no pest activity in traps, white-glove check clean
THEN PLANT READY - continue production
IF Pest activity found in ANY trap (live insects, webbing, rodent droppings)
THEN STOP production in that area. Identify and remove the source (usually a forgotten spill, a hidden flour pocket in a machine skirt, or a raw-material bag). Deep-clean and sanitise the area, add traps, call the contractor for an emergency visit, inspect ALL raw material and finished stock in that area, and log the incident. Do not restart until traps are clean for 3 consecutive days.
IF A cleaning step was missed (no signature)
THEN Do it now, before the next run. If production already ran on an unverified clean, assess the product: was any open product exposed? If yes, hold it for QC review.
IF Non-food-grade chemical found in the plant, or a chemical stored near food
THEN Remove it immediately, check whether any product could have been contaminated, and if there is any doubt, destroy the product. Re-train and re-lock the chemical store.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ Dry sweeping instead of vacuuming
→ Flour dust hangs in the air for hours and settles into open product and onto 'clean' surfaces. Also a dust-explosion risk in enclosed spaces.
✗ Pest traps installed but never checked
→ The trap is a monitoring tool; an unchecked trap is decoration.
✗ Rodent bait inside the food building
→ A poisoned rat dies inside your store and contaminates everything. Bait stations go OUTSIDE, traps go inside.
✗ Flour left in machine skirt seals
→ It turns into a beetle nursery in 2-3 weeks. The sifter and blender seals are the usual hiding places.
✗ Chemicals stored next to packaging material
→ One leak and you destroy a month of pouches and possibly the product.
S22  —  People, Uniforms, Personal Hygiene & Training  | ALL staff, contractors, visitors - everyone who enters the plant | Ongoing
Purpose
Every control in this document is executed by a human being. This stage makes sure that human is healthy, clean, trained and accountable - and it is the stage most first-time founders under-invest in.
Inputs
Uniforms, hairnets, aprons, closed footwear, handwash station, medical fitness certificates, training records, the SOP file
Outputs
A trained, medically fit, correctly dressed team with signed training records and a documented hygiene rule that is actually enforced
Critical parameters
Medical fitness on file and annual | visitor log at the door | hairnet + apron + closed footwear, always | zero jewellery, zero phones in production | handwash on entry and after every contamination event | blue waterproof plaster + glove for any wound | induction + monthly toolbox + annual test + station certification
Automation level
MANUAL (100%) - and appropriately so
How to automate it
Nothing to automate. The 'technology' here is a printed SOP card, a laminated poster, a sign-in book, a blue-plaster box, a hands-free handwash station (Rs 6,000-15,000), uniforms and hairnets (Rs 800-1,500 per person per year), and a training calendar in your phone. Total cost: under Rs 25,000. Total risk reduction: enormous.
Machines / equipment
Handwash station (hands-free) + soap dispensers + paper towels | blue waterproof plasters + food-grade gloves | uniforms, aprons, hairnets, beard snoods, closed footwear | phone locker | visitor log book | laminated SOP cards at every station
Manual work remaining
Owner/manager, ongoing. 4 h induction per new joiner; 30 min/month toolbox; 2 h/year refresher per person.
Quality checks
Daily dress-code and hygiene check at the door | monthly training attendance | annual test pass rate | medical file audited yearly

Step by step

  1. 1. MEDICAL FITNESS: every person who handles open food gets a pre-employment medical check including a stool test, and an annual repeat. Keep the certificates on file. Anyone with a skin infection on the hands, an eye/ear/nose discharge, vomiting, diarrhoea or jaundice is EXCLUDED from the production area until cleared - no discussion, no exceptions, even for the owner's brother.
  2. 2. VISITOR / STAFF LOG at the door: name, purpose, time in, time out, and confirmation that they were given a hairnet and apron and told the rules. An auditor asks for this on day one.
  3. 3. UNIFORM AND DRESS CODE, enforced at the door: clean apron or uniform (changed daily, and always changed after using the toilet), hairnet covering ALL hair (including a beard snood for beards), closed non-slip footwear dedicated to the plant (never worn outside), a face mask in the packing and sprouting rooms, and no gloves needed for dry flour handling but food-grade gloves for any wet/sprouted handling and for packing.
  4. 4. ABSOLUTE PROHIBITIONS inside production: jewellery of any kind (rings, bangles, earrings, chains, watches, fitness bands), nail polish, false or long nails, perfume/aftershave, mobile phones, eating, drinking, chewing gum or tobacco, spitting, and smoking anywhere on the premises. Provide a lockable phone shelf and a designated eating area OUTSIDE production - then you have no excuse to allow it inside.
  5. 5. HAND WASHING - install a proper station (hands-free tap, liquid soap in a dispenser, a nail brush, single-use paper towels, a waste bin, and a poster showing the 6-step method). Wash and dry hands: on entering production, after using the toilet, after handling raw grain or waste, after eating, after touching the face/hair/phone, after handling cash or a delivery challan, and after any cleaning task. Sanitise with 70% alcohol before handling open flour or a pouch interior.
  6. 6. WOUNDS: any cut or abrasion on the hand must be covered with a BRIGHT BLUE waterproof plaster (blue so it is visible if it falls off - never a skin-coloured one) PLUS a food-grade glove. If the wound is infected or weeping, the person does not handle food.
  7. 7. TRAINING - build it, do not improvise it: (a) a 4-hour INDUCTION for every new joiner covering personal hygiene, the plant layout and material flow, their specific stage SOP, the critical parameters for their stage, what to do when something goes wrong, and how to fill in a record; (b) a 30-minute MONTHLY toolbox talk on one topic (rotating through the 22 stages); (c) an ANNUAL refresher with a written 20-question test - pass mark 80%, and retrain anyone who fails; (d) specific hands-on certification for the three critical stations: sprouting, roasting, and filling/sealing - a person is 'certified' only after they have run 5 supervised batches correctly and their trainer has signed off.
  8. 8. Give every operator a LAMINATED SOP CARD for their own station: the steps, the critical numbers, a photo of what GOOD looks like and a photo of what BAD looks like, and the 'if this, then that' decision gate. A laminated card at the machine is worth ten training sessions.
  9. 9. ACCOUNTABILITY: put the operator's name on the batch card. People who sign their work do it better. Also record who VERIFIED, separately from who DID.
  10. 10. INCENTIVISE QUALITY, NOT JUST VOLUME: if you pay only for output you will get output. Run a simple monthly quality score per person (records complete, no deviations, housekeeping score, zero complaints traceable to their station) and tie a small bonus to it.
  11. 11. Keep the TRAINING RECORD file: attendance sheets, test papers, certification sign-offs, and the training calendar for the year.

Decision gates (if / then / else)

IF Person is medically fit, correctly dressed, trained and certified for their station
THEN ALLOWED IN PRODUCTION
IF Any wound, infection, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice or respiratory discharge
THEN EXCLUDE from food handling until medically cleared. Reassign to a non-food-contact task (stores, dispatch paperwork) if possible.
IF A person arrives wearing jewellery, or with long/polished nails
THEN Remove or cover it at the door, or do not enter. Enforce it on the first day and you will never have to enforce it again.
IF A new joiner has not completed induction
THEN They may observe but may not touch product or records. Schedule induction before their first shift, not after.
IF An operator fails the annual test
THEN Retrain within 7 days and re-test. Until they pass, they work under supervision at that station.

Common failure modes and the fix

✗ The founder breaks the rules 'just this once'
→ The rule is dead from that moment. You are the standard.
✗ No medical records
→ An FSSAI finding, and a real risk of a typhoid carrier handling your sprouted flour.
✗ Jewellery and phones allowed
→ A ring falls into a 500 g pouch. A phone is the dirtiest object in the building.
✗ Training done once, verbally, and never recorded
→ You cannot prove competence to an auditor, and the new helper learns by guessing.
✗ Paying only for volume
→ Operators rush the roast, skip the seal test and overfill. Pay a little for quality and you get quality.

The key insight. 19 of 22 stages are shared by all ten SKUs. Only sprouting/drying (2 SKUs + 2 mix components), dehusking (1 SKU, deferred) and staging/blending (3 SKUs) are family-specific — and blending needs just ONE new machine, the ribbon blender, for your three highest-margin SKUs. The pulveriser, roaster, sifter, filler and sealer are each used by 10 of 10 — buy them well. The dehuller is used by 1 of 10 — defer it.

Machines — what to buy, when, and what it costs

Indicative prices, India, September 2026, exclusive of GST and freight. Get three quotes per machine and demand a live video demo with your own grain before paying.

PHASE 1Destoner cum Grader cum Aspirator (combined cleaner)
S03 Cleaning		Capacity 100-250 kg/h; contact parts SS304; 1.5-3 HP; single- or three-phase; 3 sieves (interchangeable for ragi / jowar-bajra / kuttu / rajgira); aspiration with a cyclone + dust bag; stone reject cup; mounted on a frame with wheels. PHASE 1Tray dryer / food dehydrator, 12-24 trays, SS304, PID controlled
S05 Drying		12 trays (~12-25 kg wet load) or 24 trays (~25-60 kg wet load); trays AND chamber SS304; digital PID controller 30-110 C; circulation fan + adjustable exhaust damper; separate over-temperature safety cut-out; door gasket that actually seals; 3-6 kW single/three phase35,000 – 180,000Drying is the bottleneck of the sprouted SKUs: it takes 6-9 hours and nothing else can happen until it finishes. DEFERMillet dehuller cum polisher - DEFER TO PHASE 2

Revisit only when bajra volume crosses ~150 kg/day. Kuttu and rajgira are always bought dehusked - no dehuller needed for them.Weekly: inspect the abrasive roll/emery cone for wear (a glazed roll stops dehusking), clean the aspirator duct, check belt tension.
